- [2026 operator census computed from the repo's scraped catalogue (shows.json)](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/blob/main/data/normalized/shows.json)

## Open questions

- **Would the Listings API approve us, and on what terms?** Whether Fringe
  approval would be granted to a product that also shows availability badges
  scraped from edfringe.com — and whether blending the two sources in one
  product is licence-compliant at all — is unresolved and decides the
  architecture. One email to Festivals Edinburgh covers this *and* the
  static-file question already open on the festival-season page.
- **Does Tikketr/equ have any non-public partner API?** Nothing public exists;
  a private capability cannot be ruled out. The Society's arts-industry
  accreditation channel was also not examined.
- **Would any operator actually grant a small site an agent agreement?** No
  operator publishes agent terms or rates; only asking answers it. Red61 VIA
  agent access terms are likewise unpublished.
- **How do venue Red61 instances sync with Tikketr since the platform split?**
  Assembly says its box office "syncs live" with the Society's; the mechanism
  (and what it means for our availability data's freshness) is undocumented.
- **The true size of the PBH unregistered gap.** ~800 own-site listings vs 183
  registered shows is page-count arithmetic, not a confirmed count.
- **The census's name-matching caveat.** 294 venue codes carry shows vs 301
  registered venue records; the 171-venue tail was grouped by hand-checked
  substring rules. A registration-data cross-check (operator field, if the
  GraphQL exposes one) would firm it up.
- **Storm ID's 2027 scope.** Whether the new site replaces the Tikketr
  ticketing engine (breaking the scraper) or only the web front-end is not
  stated anywhere accessible.

## Growth log

- **2026-07-31** — page created. Seeded from an 11-agent research pass
  (5 web-research topics each adversarially fact-checked, plus a local census
  computed from the repo's own scraped catalogue): the Society-vs-venues
  architecture and the ≥25% allocation model (explaining
  `NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE`); edfest.com identified as the seven big
  operators' own storefront via Showcatcher Ltd; the 24-family provider census
  with its 171-venue tail and the PBH unregistered-show gap; the verified
  absence of any affiliate/agent/API selling route anywhere in the ecosystem;
  and the listings-source ranking — official Listings API as the only licensed
  catalogue alternative (approval-gated, availability-blind, edfringe-only
  linking), Traverse's public Spektrix API and Summerhall's open WP API as the
  two genuine venue-feed exceptions, Data Thistle as the only paid aggregator
  with real coverage. Two initial research claims were refuted in verification
  and corrected here (venue feeds do exist — Traverse/Summerhall; "no public
  availability source" is false for Traverse specifically). All claims cited.
  Requirements implications (monetisation ceiling, scrape-replacement
  architecture) left for human review.

1	# Audience divergence — the live crowd vs the trip planners
2	
3	EdFringeNow now points at two decisions with two front ends: *Fringe Discover*
4	(the mobile-first home site, "what can I make right now") and the planner at
5	`/plan` (desktop-first, "which of my favourites can I catch, on which dates").
6	This page exists to hold the evidence that **the two do not reduce to one set of
7	requirements** — where they pull apart, where they actively conflict, and the
8	narrow spine they genuinely share.
9	
10	It is research, not requirements: nothing here is a decision. The requirements
11	implication (two tracks rather than one) is for a human to promote into
12	`product-wiki/product-requirements/`.
13	
14	## Key insights
15	
16	- The two surfaces do not reduce to one set of requirements. That is the finding.
17	- The planner packs the day; the evidence says a good day is half empty.
18	- One sold-out flag: a fact for the live surface, a decaying guess for the planner.
19	- Live asks the user for nothing. The planner needs a CSV from a third-party extension.
20	- "When should I come?" has no live version — and no competitor answers it.
21	- What they truly share is small: the catalogue, the travel model, the promise.
22	- The plan-to-live handover is the one shared feature worth building. It does not exist.
23	
24	## The two crowds in a line each
25	
26	- **Live, in-festival.** On the ground in Edinburgh during 7–31 August, deciding
27	  for the next hour or two. A third of the Fringe audience lives in Edinburgh and
28	  has no trip to plan at all; most ticket buyers buy a single ticket.
29	- **Trip planners.** Two thirds of the audience come from outside Edinburgh,
30	  choose dates and beds, and assemble a favourites list months before August —
31	  the 2026 programme launched on 4 June, and audiences now engage with the
32	  festival long before it starts.
33	
34	They may be the same person in different states — the Fringe CEO's "rule of
35	thirds" describes one visitor pre-planning about a third of their time and
36	leaving the rest open. That does not make it one requirement set; it makes the
37	handover between the two surfaces a design problem in its own right.
38	
39	## Where they diverge
40	
41	| Axis | Live surface | Planner |
42	|---|---|---|
43	| **Horizon** | the next 1–2 hours | a stay chosen weeks out, then re-tuned |
44	| **Origin** | device location, "here, now" | no useful location; an accommodation base at best |
45	| **Taste input** | zero-effort defaults, genre chips, free/paid | an explicit favourites list built elsewhere, at high effort |
46	| **Correctness** | is this *still* catchable — a live fact | will this *be* catchable — a forecast that decays |
47	| **Objective** | one good, reachable option now | a whole trip's worth, and which dates make it possible |
48	| **Cost of error** | a wasted walk, a late entrance | non-refundable tickets, travel and beds booked around a wrong plan |
49	| **Device & context** | phone, outdoors, one hand, sunlight, patchy signal | desktop, indoors, deliberate, wide canvas |
50	| **Time to value** | seconds; typing is failure | minutes of deliberate work is acceptable |
51	| **State** | stateless — the answer expires with the hour | persistent — favourites, window, itinerary, exports (CSV/ICS) |
52	| **Season** | only 7–31 August, and value shifts across the run | February–July, peaking after each programme drop |
53	| **Success** | "I chose something and I made it" | "N of my favourites got caught, and the days were liveable" |
54	
55	## Requirements that actively conflict
56	
57	These are the places where satisfying one crowd well makes the other worse.
58	Naming them is the point of this page.
59	
60	1. **Pack the day vs leave the day open.** The planner's allocator is an
61	   earliest-finish-first greedy — it maximises the number of shows placed. The
62	   audience evidence points the other way: two to three shows a day is the pace
63	   commonly advised, visitors who combined structured planning with open time
64	   reported higher satisfaction than over-schedulers, and the rule of thirds asks
65	   for roughly a third of the time planned. A planner that fills the day
66	   optimally also destroys the gaps the live surface serves. The two surfaces can
67	   be jointly optimal only if the planner's objective is *not* "maximum shows".
68	2. **Live truth vs planning truth, from one catalogue.** Both surfaces read the
69	   same `data/normalized/shows.json`. For the live surface, sold-out /
70	   started-already is a *fact* and staleness is the core failure mode. For the
71	   planner, the same field is a *forecast* about a date weeks away, which decays
72	   in the opposite direction (shows sell out as August approaches; walk-ups are
73	   easy in week one and scarce in weeks two and three). Identical data, two
74	   incompatible honesty obligations — the planner arguably must show "may sell
75	   out before you book" where the live surface must show "gone".
76	3. **Zero input vs high-effort input.** The brief's live target is "a brand-new
77	   user with zero taps already sees useful results". The planner's front door is
78	   a CSV export the user produces on another site — and, as far as the research
79	   shows, via a third-party browser extension. One surface's core virtue is
80	   asking nothing; the other's is asking for something quite hard to obtain.
81	4. **Personalisation model.** Live personalisation is coarse taste (ten festival
82	   genres, free/paid) applied to whatever is reachable. Planner personalisation
83	   is an explicit, already-curated favourites set — a different data model, a
84	   different privacy posture (the planner keeps parsed favourites in
85	   `localStorage` for three days; the live surface keeps nothing), and different
86	   recommendation logic. Merging them into "one personalisation system" would
87	   serve neither.
88	5. **What "optimise" even means.** Live: maximise the chance the user goes and
89	   enjoys one show inside a slack budget. Planner: maximise favourites caught
90	   across a window — and, upstream of that, choose the window. The planner's
91	   *most valuable* question ("when should I come?") has no live analogue at all,
92	   and no profiled competitor answers it.
93	6. **Which constraints are even visible.** The live surface's binding constraint
94	   is travel time to the next commitment. The planner's real binding constraint
95	   may not be shows at all: over half of would-be attendees reportedly could not
96	   find affordable accommodation within a 90-minute commute, so dates are chosen
97	   against beds. `/plan`'s "pick my best dates" scores windows purely on show
98	   catchability — optimising a variable the user may not be free to move.
99	7. **Failure of the map.** Live, a map answers "where is that relative to me".
100	   In the planner, there is no "me" — the map's job becomes clustering and
101	   walkability across a day, which is a different visualisation with different
102	   requirements (and the reason the planner's schedule draws travel legs rather
103	   than a map).
104	
105	## What the two genuinely share
106	
107	Small, and worth keeping small deliberately:
108	
109	- **One catalogue and one venue geometry** — the scraped `shows.json` /
110	  `venues.json`, already shared, plus the haversine + per-mode travel model in
111	  `plan/lib/travel.js` and the `UK_BOUNDS` helper both front ends import.
112	- **Honesty about data gaps** — no ticket prices beyond free/paid, no live seat
113	  counts beyond a sold-out flag. Neither surface may imply data we don't have.

# Audience divergence — the live crowd vs the trip planners

EdFringeNow now points at two decisions with two front ends: *Fringe Discover*
(the mobile-first home site, "what can I make right now") and the planner at
`/plan` (desktop-first, "which of my favourites can I catch, on which dates").
This page exists to hold the evidence that **the two do not reduce to one set of
requirements** — where they pull apart, where they actively conflict, and the
narrow spine they genuinely share.

It is research, not requirements: nothing here is a decision. The requirements
implication (two tracks rather than one) is for a human to promote into
`product-wiki/product-requirements/`.

## Key insights

- The two surfaces do not reduce to one set of requirements. That is the finding.
- The planner packs the day; the evidence says a good day is half empty.
- One sold-out flag: a fact for the live surface, a decaying guess for the planner.
- Live asks the user for nothing. The planner needs a CSV from a third-party extension.
- "When should I come?" has no live version — and no competitor answers it.
- What they truly share is small: the catalogue, the travel model, the promise.
- The plan-to-live handover is the one shared feature worth building. It does not exist.

## The two crowds in a line each

- **Live, in-festival.** On the ground in Edinburgh during 7–31 August, deciding
  for the next hour or two. A third of the Fringe audience lives in Edinburgh and
  has no trip to plan at all; most ticket buyers buy a single ticket.
- **Trip planners.** Two thirds of the audience come from outside Edinburgh,
  choose dates and beds, and assemble a favourites list months before August —
  the 2026 programme launched on 4 June, and audiences now engage with the
  festival long before it starts.

They may be the same person in different states — the Fringe CEO's "rule of
thirds" describes one visitor pre-planning about a third of their time and
leaving the rest open. That does not make it one requirement set; it makes the
handover between the two surfaces a design problem in its own right.

## Where they diverge

| Axis | Live surface | Planner |
|---|---|---|
| **Horizon** | the next 1–2 hours | a stay chosen weeks out, then re-tuned |
| **Origin** | device location, "here, now" | no useful location; an accommodation base at best |
| **Taste input** | zero-effort defaults, genre chips, free/paid | an explicit favourites list built elsewhere, at high effort |
| **Correctness** | is this *still* catchable — a live fact | will this *be* catchable — a forecast that decays |
| **Objective** | one good, reachable option now | a whole trip's worth, and which dates make it possible |
| **Cost of error** | a wasted walk, a late entrance | non-refundable tickets, travel and beds booked around a wrong plan |
| **Device & context** | phone, outdoors, one hand, sunlight, patchy signal | desktop, indoors, deliberate, wide canvas |
| **Time to value** | seconds; typing is failure | minutes of deliberate work is acceptable |
| **State** | stateless — the answer expires with the hour | persistent — favourites, window, itinerary, exports (CSV/ICS) |
| **Season** | only 7–31 August, and value shifts across the run | February–July, peaking after each programme drop |
| **Success** | "I chose something and I made it" | "N of my favourites got caught, and the days were liveable" |

## Requirements that actively conflict

These are the places where satisfying one crowd well makes the other worse.
Naming them is the point of this page.

1. **Pack the day vs leave the day open.** The planner's allocator is an
   earliest-finish-first greedy — it maximises the number of shows placed. The
   audience evidence points the other way: two to three shows a day is the pace
   commonly advised, visitors who combined structured planning with open time
   reported higher satisfaction than over-schedulers, and the rule of thirds asks
   for roughly a third of the time planned. A planner that fills the day
   optimally also destroys the gaps the live surface serves. The two surfaces can
   be jointly optimal only if the planner's objective is *not* "maximum shows".
2. **Live truth vs planning truth, from one catalogue.** Both surfaces read the
   same `data/normalized/shows.json`. For the live surface, sold-out /
   started-already is a *fact* and staleness is the core failure mode. For the
   planner, the same field is a *forecast* about a date weeks away, which decays
   in the opposite direction (shows sell out as August approaches; walk-ups are
   easy in week one and scarce in weeks two and three). Identical data, two
   incompatible honesty obligations — the planner arguably must show "may sell
   out before you book" where the live surface must show "gone".
3. **Zero input vs high-effort input.** The brief's live target is "a brand-new
   user with zero taps already sees useful results". The planner's front door is
   a CSV export the user produces on another site — and, as far as the research
   shows, via a third-party browser extension. One surface's core virtue is
   asking nothing; the other's is asking for something quite hard to obtain.
4. **Personalisation model.** Live personalisation is coarse taste (ten festival
   genres, free/paid) applied to whatever is reachable. Planner personalisation
   is an explicit, already-curated favourites set — a different data model, a
   different privacy posture (the planner keeps parsed favourites in
   `localStorage` for three days; the live surface keeps nothing), and different
   recommendation logic. Merging them into "one personalisation system" would
   serve neither.
5. **What "optimise" even means.** Live: maximise the chance the user goes and
   enjoys one show inside a slack budget. Planner: maximise favourites caught
   across a window — and, upstream of that, choose the window. The planner's
   *most valuable* question ("when should I come?") has no live analogue at all,
   and no profiled competitor answers it.
6. **Which constraints are even visible.** The live surface's binding constraint
   is travel time to the next commitment. The planner's real binding constraint
   may not be shows at all: over half of would-be attendees reportedly could not
   find affordable accommodation within a 90-minute commute, so dates are chosen
   against beds. `/plan`'s "pick my best dates" scores windows purely on show
   catchability — optimising a variable the user may not be free to move.
7. **Failure of the map.** Live, a map answers "where is that relative to me".
   In the planner, there is no "me" — the map's job becomes clustering and
   walkability across a day, which is a different visualisation with different
   requirements (and the reason the planner's schedule draws travel legs rather
   than a map).

## What the two genuinely share

Small, and worth keeping small deliberately:

- **One catalogue and one venue geometry** — the scraped `shows.json` /
  `venues.json`, already shared, plus the haversine + per-mode travel model in
  `plan/lib/travel.js` and the `UK_BOUNDS` helper both front ends import.
- **Honesty about data gaps** — no ticket prices beyond free/paid, no live seat
  counts beyond a sold-out flag. Neither surface may imply data we don't have.
- **The same emotional promise** — the overwhelm lifting. 37% of audiences
  reported struggling to pick a show; both surfaces exist to answer that, at
  different distances from the decision.
- **A handover, in one direction.** The planner's deliberate gaps are the live
  surface's demand. Nothing today connects them (no shared favourites, no "your
  plan says you're free until 19:00"), and that connection is the one place where
  a *shared* requirement would be justified.

## Sources

- [How to use your audience data with a purpose: the Edinburgh Festival Fringe (Thrive)](https://wewillthrive.co.uk/resources/case-studies/how-to-use-your-audience-data-with-a-purpose-the-edinburgh-festival-fringe/) — a third of the audience lives in Edinburgh; two thirds of ticket buyers bought one ticket; 37% struggled to pick a show.
- [Fringe 2026 — How the Audience Has Changed (The Edinburgh Reporter)](https://theedinburghreporter.co.uk/2026/05/fringe-2026-how-the-audience-has-changed/) — months-ahead engagement; the CEO's "rule of thirds".
- [Edinburgh Fringe 2026: First-Timer's Planning Guide (Discover Edinburgh Fringe)](https://discoveredinburghfringe.com/en/blog/edinburgh-fringe-2026-first-timers-planning-guide) — two-to-three shows a day; walk-ups easy in week one, scarce in weeks two and three.
- [Ten tips for Fringe first-timers in 2026 (Edinburgh Festival City)](https://www.edinburghfestivalcity.com/inspiration/128-five-tips-for-fringe-first-timers) — leave travel time between venues.
- [Late night transport and 'live dashboard' could solve Edinburgh's festival accommodation crisis (The Scotsman)](https://www.scotsman.com/arts-and-culture/late-night-transport-and-live-dashboard-could-solve-edinburghs-festival-accommodation-crisis-5239090) — over half unable to find affordable accommodation within a 90-minute commute.
- [The 2026 Edinburgh Festival Fringe programme is now live (edfringe.com)](https://www.edfringe.com/about-us/news-and-blog/mixitup-with-the-2026-edinburgh-festival-fringe-programme/) — 4 June 2026 launch; 7–31 August dates.
- [EdFringe Favourites to CSV (Chrome Web Store)](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/edfringe-favourites-to-cs/ebbiecdkhoclnlgfibfhhnpfhmmgdbcc) — the third-party export path the planner's intake depends on.
- [Plan My Fringe — Help](https://www.planmyfringe.co.uk/Help.aspx) — the competing planner's constraint set (budget, walking speed, per-day max, minimum gap, meal and sleep minimums).
- [EdFringeNow — Fringe Discover product & experience brief (`docs/product-spec.md`)](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/blob/main/docs/product-spec.md) — the live surface's stated inputs, outputs and zero-input target.
- [EdFringeNow — Fringe Planner README (`plan/README.md`)](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/blob/main/plan/README.md) — the planner's intake, engine, controls, exports and three-day `localStorage` retention.
- [EdFringeNow — planner scheduling engine (`plan/lib/engine.js`)](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/blob/main/plan/lib/engine.js) — the earliest-finish-first greedy that maximises placed shows.

## Open questions

- **Is the shared person real, or two populations?** No evidence found either way
  on how many planner users are also in Edinburgh mid-festival. If the overlap is
  large, the handover (plan → live) is the highest-value unbuilt feature; if it
  is small, the two products should probably diverge further, not converge.
- **What should the planner optimise for?** "Most shows placed" is contradicted
  by the satisfaction evidence, but "leave a third open" has no measured optimum
  either. What does a *good* Fringe day look like, quantitatively?
- **How does availability actually decay between planning and August?** Nothing
  cited yet on sell-out rates by week or by show popularity — which decides how
  honest the planner can be about a plan made in June.
- **Does the accommodation constraint dominate date choice?** If it does, date
  scoring needs a second input the product doesn't have.
- **Is there a third crowd?** Artists, reviewers and industry are all in the same
  data with different needs (own-show scheduling, review runs); nothing here has
  looked at them.
- **Does the divergence extend to the scraper?** The live surface wants frequent
  refresh of status for today; the planner wants a stable whole-festival
  snapshot. Whether one data pipeline serves both well is unexamined.

## Growth log

- **2026-07-28** — initial seed, created deliberately after the owner asked for
  research covering both the live in-festival crowd and the trip-planning crowd
  without assuming a single requirement set. Compiled the divergence axes, the
  seven concrete requirement conflicts, and the shared spine, from the audience
  evidence gathered on the market-and-audience page plus the repo's two surfaces.
  Sources cited.
- **2026-07-29** — added the page's `## Key insights` header: seven terse lines
  distilled from what the page already says (the non-reducibility finding, the
  sharpest conflicts, the small shared spine, the handover). Header only: no
  claim, citation or open question changed.

cd /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-EdFringeNow/26ae9aec-41c3-56e6-b289-00b96b2f07a2/scratchpad && python3 - <<'EOF'
import re, html
raw = open('comedy-festivals.html', encoding='utf-8', errors='replace').read()
# Drop scripts/styles, then strip tags but keep heading/list structure markers
raw = re.sub(r'<script.*?</script>', '', raw, flags=re.S)
raw = re.sub(r'<style.*?</style>', '', raw, flags=re.S)
# Mark headings and list items so structure survives
raw = re.sub(r'<(h[1-6])[^>]*>', r'\n\n[\1] ', raw)
raw = re.sub(r'<li[^>]*>', '\n - ', raw)
raw = re.sub(r'<(p|tr|div|br)[^>]*>', '\n', raw)
# Keep hrefs next to their anchor text
raw = re.sub(r'<a[^>]*href="([^"]+)"[^>]*>', r' <<\1>> ', raw)
text = re.sub(r'<[^>]+>', '', raw)
text = html.unescape(text)
lines = [l.strip() for l in text.splitlines()]
lines = [l for l in lines if l]
open('comedy-festivals.txt','w').write('\n'.join(lines))
print(len(lines), 'lines')
EOF

input.description: Research AU/NZ comedy festivals
input.prompt:
You are a research agent for a product-wiki pass on comedy festivals. Your territory: Australia / New Zealand. You research festivals and return a structured, citation-backed report as your final message. You must NOT write or edit any repo files — the report is your only output.

## Festivals to research (in priority order)
1. **Melbourne International Comedy Festival** (MICF) — official site comedyfestival.com.au. The most important one in your set: reportedly one of the largest comedy festivals in the world.
2. **Sydney Comedy Festival** — sydneycomedyfest.com.au
3. **New Zealand International Comedy Festival** — comedyfestival.co.nz (runs in Auckland AND Wellington — how does the two-city model work?)
4. **Adelaide Fringe** — adelaidefringe.com.au. Our wiki already covers its scale (1,648 shows / 562 venues / ~1.08M tickets 2026, open access, "Mad March" cluster). You only need: (a) its ticketing platform (FringeTIX? who runs it, is it central-basket, per-venue?), (b) organizer (who runs Adelaide Fringe Inc?), (c) what share of its programme is comedy, (d) any signs of a machine-readable programme/API.
5. **Perth Comedy Festival** (if it still exists — distinct from FRINGE WORLD Perth) — brief.

## Per-festival dossier fields (collect ALL of these; write NOT FOUND where you can't find it)
- **Organizer**: legal entity / nonprofit vs promoter vs government; stability (years running, any recent ownership drama).
- **Recurrence**: annual? same city every year? same venues year over year? since what year? Any one-off or roving pattern.
- **Scale**: number of shows, venues, performances, run length in days; tickets/attendance if published. Distinguish LAUNCH announcements from DELIVERED totals where possible (festivals keep registering shows after launch).
- **Show model**: does a show run repeatedly across the festival (Edinburgh-style: one show ≈ 20-25 performances of the same hour) or is it one-night showcases/galas? Curated (invited/programmed) vs open-access (anyone who registers is in)?
- **Venue geography**: how many venues, concentrated in a walkable core vs spread across the city; named venue hubs.
- **Scheduling clash reality**: at peak, how many shows run in parallel? Is "which of these can I make tonight" a real problem for a visitor (fringe-like) or is it a lineup-picking problem with few stages (music-festival-like)?
- **Ticketing**: who sells tickets (central festival box office vs per-venue vs Ticketmaster/Ticketek/Eventbrite)? One basket for all shows? Booking fees? Identify the actual ticketing platform/vendor if you can (look at ticket-purchase URLs, e.g. Red61, Ferve, Ticketek, SeatGeek, sabo…).
- **Data reachability**: is the programme machine-readable? Fetch the official site's programme/what's-on page with curl and look at the HTML: is it server-rendered, or does it load JSON from an API endpoint you can name? Check /sitemap.xml. Name concrete endpoints if you find them. Do NOT build a scraper — just identify what a scrape would target.
- **Concurrent festivals**: other festivals in the same city overlapping the same dates that make the city a bigger draw (e.g. Melbourne in late March/April: what else is on? Sydney in April/May? Auckland in May?).
- **Official planner/app**: does the festival ship an app or planner feature (favourites, itinerary)? Any known third-party planner tools for this festival?

## Method
- Outbound HTTPS works through a pre-configured proxy: `curl -sS -m 30 <url>` works for most sites. Fetch official pages (homepage, what's-on/programme page, one show page, ticketing/FAQ page) into your scratchpad and read them. This is the preferred evidence.
- Use WebSearch for scale figures, attendance, press coverage, organizer background. Attribute figures to the publisher the snippet names as origin.
- EVERY claim in your report must carry its source URL inline. Mark clearly which claims come from a fetched page vs a search snippet.
- Never invent. NOT FOUND is a good answer. A number seen in several search results is still one source repeated — attribute to the origin publisher.
- Sanity-check dates against 2026 editions where possible (today is 2026-09-01; MICF ran March 25–Apr 19, Sydney Apr 13–May 17, NZ May 1–24 per our source list).

## Output format
Final message = the full report, markdown. Per festival: a dossier with the fields above as a compact bullet list, each bullet citing its URL. End with: (a) a one-line "fringe-like ↔ showcase-like" verdict per festival with the 2-3 facts that decide it, (b) a list of every source URL used. Keep the whole report under ~350 lines.

input.prompt:
You are a research agent for a product-wiki pass on comedy festivals. Your territory: the **Just For Laughs (JFL) empire**. You research and return a structured, citation-backed report as your final message. You must NOT write or edit any repo files — the report is your only output.

Our source list (fromthecomicscomic.com/comedy-festivals/, 2026) shows JFL events in: Vancouver (Feb 12–22, jflvancouver.com), Belgium (March 23–29, hahaha.com/public/festivals/belgium-951/), Montreal flagship (July 15–26, montreal.hahaha.com), Quebec City (July 22–Aug 2, hahaha.com/public/festivals/quebec-963/), Paris (Sept 17–20, hahaha.com/public/festivals/paris-962/), Toronto (Sept 24–Oct 3, toronto.hahaha.com), Sydney (Nov 9–22, justforlaughs.sydney), Singapore (tbd, jflsingapore.com), Bermuda (Feb 17–20 2027, comedyevent.bm).

## Questions to answer (all citation-backed)
1. **Ownership & stability**: JFL's parent (Groupe Juste pour rire) filed for creditor protection in March 2024 and the 2024 Montreal festival was cancelled. Who owns it now (ComediHa? someone else?), what happened to the 2025 and 2026 Montreal editions, and how stable is the franchise? This is the single most important question in your set — a planner product needs to know if a festival is a durable annual anchor or a brand in receivership.
2. **Franchise structure**: which of the city editions are run by the JFL organization itself vs licensed to local promoters (e.g. Sydney's appears to be a separate promoter — check justforlaughs.sydney's fine print; Vancouver was formerly JFL NorthWest; Toronto's history)? Which are long-running annuals vs new/one-off experiments (Belgium? Paris? Singapore? Bermuda?)?
3. **Montreal flagship dossier** (deepest): 2026 scale (number of shows, venues, run length); the model — big galas + club shows + free outdoor programming (Quartier des Spectacles); English vs French programming (it's really two festivals: Just pour rire + JFL); what happened to OFF-JFL/Zoofest; the show model (one-night showcases vs repeated runs); venue geography (concentrated in Quartier des Spectacles?); scheduling clash reality at peak.
4. **Per-city mini-dossiers** (Vancouver, Toronto, Sydney, and briefly Quebec/Paris/Belgium/Singapore/Bermuda): dates, scale (# shows/venues), annual since when, organizer, venue spread, showcase-vs-run model.
5. **Ticketing**: what platform does hahaha.com use (fetch a show page and look at the purchase flow — Ticketmaster? own system?); per-city differences (Sydney on Ticketek?); single basket?
6. **Data reachability**: fetch montreal.hahaha.com's lineup/schedule page with curl — is the programme server-rendered or API-driven? Name concrete JSON endpoints if visible. Check /sitemap.xml. Do NOT build a scraper.
7. **Concurrent festivals**: what else runs in Montreal overlapping July 15–26 (Jazz Fest ends ~July 4; Montréal Complètement Cirque? Fantasia Film Festival? Osheaga is Aug)? Same for Toronto late Sept (TIFF is earlier Sept — overlap?) and Vancouver Feb.
8. **Official planner/app**: does JFL ship an app/planner? Any third-party planner tools for JFL?

## Method
- Outbound HTTPS works through a pre-configured proxy: `curl -sS -m 30 <url>` works for most sites. Fetch official pages (hahaha.com festival pages, a show page, FAQ/ticketing page) into your scratchpad and read them. Preferred evidence.
- WebSearch for the bankruptcy/ownership story (there will be solid press: CBC, Montreal Gazette, Variety, Deadline) and scale figures. Attribute figures to the origin publisher.
- EVERY claim carries its source URL inline. Mark fetched-page evidence vs search-snippet evidence. NOT FOUND is a good answer. Never invent.

## Output format
Final message = full report, markdown. Sections: ownership story; franchise map (a table: city | dates 2026 | annual since | operator | scale | status); Montreal deep dossier; per-city notes; ticketing & data; concurrents; planner/app. One-line "fringe-like ↔ showcase-like" verdict for Montreal and for the satellite editions. End with every source URL used. Keep it under ~350 lines.

Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.

input.description: Research UK/Ireland comedy festivals
input.prompt:
You are a research agent for a product-wiki pass on comedy festivals. Your territory: **UK & Ireland (excluding the Edinburgh Fringe itself, which our wiki already covers in depth)**. You research and return a structured, citation-backed report as your final message. You must NOT write or edit any repo files — the report is your only output.

## Festivals to research (priority order)
1. **Leicester Comedy Festival** (Feb 4–22 2026, comedy-festival.co.uk) — the UK's biggest pure comedy festival; reportedly hundreds of shows across dozens of venues. Deepest dossier in your set. Organizer is reportedly a charity (Big Difference Company) — verify; there was 2025 news about its future (funding crisis / new ownership by Gloucester-based? verify what actually happened and who runs the 2026 edition).
2. **Brighton Fringe** (May 1–31, brightonfringe.org) — our wiki covers its overall scale (open access, ~400k attendances). You add: comedy's share of the programme, ticketing platform (who runs the box office; per-venue vs central), data reachability (machine-readable programme?), and the concurrent-festival cluster (Brighton Festival, The Great Escape — do they overlap?).
3. **Galway Comedy Festival** (Oct 20–26, galwaycomedyfestival.ie — check if branded "Vodafone Comedy Carnival Galway") — scale, venues, organizer.
4. **"Dublin Comedy Festival" (Sept 11–Oct 3?)** — our source list links this label to dublinwestcomedyfest.ie, which looks like a different, smaller festival (Dublin West). Untangle this: what is actually at that URL, is there a real "Dublin Comedy Festival", and does the big September thing in Dublin actually exist? Note also Dublin Fringe Festival (theatre-led, ~Sept) as the possible confusion source and as a concurrent festival.
5. **Aberdeen Comedy Festival** (Sept 19–Oct 4, run by Aberdeen Performing Arts) — brief dossier.
6. **Wells Comedy Festival** (May 22–24, wellscomfest.com) and **Machynlleth Comedy Festival** (Wales — not on our source list but the best-known UK "small town takeover" comedy festival; include it briefly and note it was missing from the tracker) — the small-town-weekend model.
7. **Greenwich Comedy Festival** (July 15–19, London — single-site big top?) and **Roundhouse Comedy Festival** (Aug 23–26, one building) — the single-venue model, brief.
8. **London Clown Festival** (May 30–Jun 13) — brief.

## Per-festival dossier fields (collect ALL; write NOT FOUND where you can't)
- **Organizer**: entity type (charity/promoter/venue), stability, years running.
- **Recurrence**: annual? same city/venues every year? since when?
- **Scale**: shows / venues / performances / run-length days; tickets or attendance if published. Distinguish launch claims from delivered totals.
- **Show model**: repeated runs of one show (Edinburgh-style) vs one-night shows? Curated vs open-access (Leicester and Brighton are reportedly open-access — verify)?
- **Venue geography**: count, walkable core vs spread.
- **Clash reality**: how many shows in parallel at peak; is scheduling a genuine visitor problem?
- **Ticketing**: central box office vs per-venue; the platform vendor if identifiable from purchase URLs (Red61? Ticketsolve? Eventotron? Little Box Office? Skiddle? Ticketmaster?); single basket?
- **Data reachability**: fetch the what's-on/programme page with curl; server-rendered vs API-driven; name concrete endpoints if visible; check /sitemap.xml. Don't build a scraper.
- **Concurrent festivals**: overlapping festivals in the same city (e.g. Brighton May cluster; Dublin September = Dublin Fringe + Dublin Theatre Festival edges; Galway October?).
- **Official planner/app** and any third-party planner tools.

## Method
- Outbound HTTPS works through a pre-configured proxy: `curl -sS -m 30 <url>` works for most sites. Fetch official pages (programme page, ticketing/FAQ, one show page). Preferred evidence.
- WebSearch for press coverage (Chortle and British Comedy Guide are the trade press for UK comedy — good sources), scale figures, the Leicester funding story. Attribute figures to origin publishers.
- EVERY claim carries its source URL inline. Mark fetched vs snippet evidence. NOT FOUND is honest. Never invent.

## Output format
Final message = full report, markdown, dossier per festival, each bullet cited. One-line "fringe-like ↔ showcase-like" verdict per festival with deciding facts. End with all source URLs. Under ~350 lines.

You are a research agent for a product-wiki pass on comedy festivals. Your territory: **the US majors**. You research and return a structured, citation-backed report as your final message. You must NOT write or edit any repo files — the report is your only output.

## Festivals to research (priority order — the first five get the deepest dossiers)
1. **SF Sketchfest** (Jan 15–Feb 1 2026, sfsketchfest.com) — reportedly one of the biggest US comedy festivals by show count; multi-week, many venues.
2. **Netflix Is A Joke Fest** (May 4–10 2026, netflixisajokefest.com, Los Angeles) — corporate-run; CHECK RECURRENCE CAREFULLY: editions were 2022, 2024, 2025… is it now annual? Is 2026 confirmed/delivered? Scale (reportedly 300+ shows across dozens of LA venues); citywide spread (LA is not walkable — what does that do to scheduling?).
3. **New York Comedy Festival** (Nov 6–15 2026, nycomedyfestival.com) — founded by Caroline Hirsch (Carolines on Broadway closed — who runs it now?); scale (~100-200 shows?); venue spread across boroughs.
4. **Moontower Comedy Festival** (Apr 8–19 2026, austintheatre.org/moontower-comedy) — run by Austin Theatre Alliance (Paramount Theatre); badge model + single tickets — the "wristband/badge" hybrid matters for our ticketing comparison.
5. **SXSW Comedy** (Mar 13–16 within SXSW, sxsw.com/festivals/comedy) — a comedy track inside a giant badge-driven multi-festival; the purest "concurrent festivals make the city the draw" case in your set.
6. Briefer dossiers: **Nashville Comedy Festival** (Apr 9–19, nashcomedyfest.com — promoter-run? Outback Presents?), **312 Comedy Festival** (Nov 5–15, Chicago, 312comedyfestival.com — new? who runs it?), **Boston Comedy Festival** (Nov 10–14), **Skankfest** (Nov 13–15, New Orleans, skankfest.com — GaS Digital; sells out on brand loyalty), **Del Close Marathon** (June 12–14, NYC, UCB improv marathon — 3 days round-the-clock), **NY Laughs Fest** (June 4–7, Union Square — free outdoor?), **San Francisco Comedy Competition** and **Seattle International Comedy Competition** (both: month-long touring competitions across a region — a structurally different shape worth 3 lines each).

## Per-festival dossier fields (collect ALL; write NOT FOUND where you can't)
- **Organizer**: promoter/corporate/nonprofit/venue; stability; years running.
- **Recurrence**: annual? same city/venues? since when? gaps/cancellations (Netflix especially).
- **Scale**: shows / venues / days; attendance if published.
- **Show model**: one-night showcases and galas (typical US model) vs repeated runs? Same comedian playing multiple nights? Curated lineup vs open submission (many US club fests take submissions — note which).
- **Venue geography**: count; walkable cluster vs car-city spread (LA/Austin/NYC differ hugely — say which).
- **Clash reality**: shows in parallel at peak; is scheduling a real visitor problem or a pick-your-headliner problem?
- **Ticketing**: central platform vs per-venue; badges/wristbands vs single tickets; vendor identifiable from purchase URLs (Ticketmaster/AXS/Eventbrite/SeatGeek/Etix/DICE/venue systems)?
- **Data reachability**: fetch the lineup/schedule page with curl; server-rendered vs API-driven; name concrete JSON endpoints if visible; check /sitemap.xml. Don't build a scraper.
- **Concurrent festivals**: anything overlapping in the same city that makes the city a bigger draw (SXSW is itself the case study — music+film+interactive+comedy in one badge).
- **Official planner/app**: SXSW has a famous schedule builder (SXSW GO) — describe it; Netflix Is A Joke app? NYCF app? Moontower schedule tools?

## Method
- Outbound HTTPS works through a pre-configured proxy: `curl -sS -m 30 <url>` works for most sites. Fetch official pages (lineup/schedule page, FAQ/ticketing page, one show page). Preferred evidence.
- WebSearch for scale figures and press (Vulture, LA Times, Variety, Deadline, Chortle cover these). Attribute figures to origin publishers.
- EVERY claim carries its source URL inline. Mark fetched vs snippet evidence. NOT FOUND is honest. Never invent.

## Output format
Final message = full report, markdown, dossier per festival, each bullet cited. One-line "fringe-like ↔ showcase-like" verdict per festival with the deciding facts. End with all source URLs. Under ~400 lines.

Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.

input.prompt:
You are a research agent for a product-wiki pass on comedy festivals. Your territory: **Canada (non-JFL) + rest of world**. You research and return a structured, citation-backed report as your final message. You must NOT write or edit any repo files — the report is your only output.

## Festivals to research
1. **Winnipeg Comedy Festival** (Apr 20–26 2026, winnipegcomedyfestival.com) — long-running; CBC TV gala tapings — how does TV production shape it?
2. **Halifax ComedyFest** (May 5–9, halifaxcomedyfest.ca) — likewise CBC-linked.
3. **Grindstone Comedy Festival** (July 2–12, Edmonton, grindstonecomedyfest.com) — 10 days; venue-run (Grindstone Theatre)? scale?
4. **Toronto Sketch Comedy Festival** (Mar 4–15, torontosketchfest.com) and **WHAT THE FESTIVAL!** (Sept 24–27, Toronto, wtfestival.ca) — brief; note Toronto also hosts JFL Toronto (researched by another agent).
5. **Great Outdoors Comedy Festival** (Aug 28–30 Vancouver stop, greatoutdoorscomedyfestival.com) — IMPORTANT STRUCTURAL CASE: it appears to be a TOURING outdoor amphitheatre series hitting multiple cities (Edmonton, Calgary, Winnipeg, Vancouver, US cities?). If so it is literally a music-festival-shaped comedy product (few stages, one show per act, roving cities) — the perfect contrast case for our taxonomy. Establish: how many cities/dates in 2026, stage count, ticketing (Ticketmaster? own?), operator (Trixstar?).
6. **Dubai Comedy Festival** (Oct 9–18, dubaicomedyfest.ae) — government-backed (Dubai Calendar / Brand Dubai?); scale; venues (Coca-Cola Arena + theatres?); one-night international acts model; ticketing (Platinumlist? Dubai Calendar?).
7. **Tokyo International Comedy Festival** (Sept 17–27, tokyocomedybar.com/festival) — run by Tokyo Comedy Bar? English-language standup scene; scale; brief.
8. **Lucille Ball Comedy Festival** (Aug 6–9, Jamestown NY, comedycenter.org/festival) — run by the National Comedy Center (a museum/institution) — the institution-anchored model; brief.

## Per-festival dossier fields (collect ALL; write NOT FOUND where you can't)
- **Organizer**: entity type (venue/nonprofit/promoter/government/broadcaster); stability; years running.
- **Recurrence**: annual? same city/venues? since when? For Great Outdoors: the roving pattern is the finding — document the city list instead.
- **Scale**: shows / venues / days; attendance if published.
- **Show model**: one-night showcases/galas vs repeated runs; curated vs submissions.
- **Venue geography**: count; walkable vs spread; for arena/outdoor events, capacity.
- **Clash reality**: parallel shows at peak — real scheduling problem or lineup-picking?
- **Ticketing**: central vs per-venue; vendor from purchase URLs (Ticketmaster/Eventbrite/Showpass/Platinumlist/…).
- **Data reachability**: fetch the schedule/lineup page with curl; server-rendered vs API-driven; concrete endpoints if visible. Don't build a scraper.
- **Concurrent festivals**: anything overlapping in the same city (e.g. Dubai October = ?, Winnipeg April = ?).
- **Official planner/app** if any.

## Method
- Outbound HTTPS works through a pre-configured proxy: `curl -sS -m 30 <url>` works for most sites. Fetch official pages (lineup/schedule, FAQ/ticketing). Preferred evidence.
- WebSearch for press and figures (CBC, local press, Chortle). Attribute figures to origin publishers.
- EVERY claim carries its source URL inline. Mark fetched vs snippet evidence. NOT FOUND is honest. Never invent.

## Output format
Final message = full report, markdown, dossier per festival, each bullet cited. One-line "fringe-like ↔ showcase-like" verdict per festival. End with all source URLs. Under ~300 lines.

You are a research agent for a product-wiki pass on comedy festivals. Your territory: **Canada (non-JFL) + rest of world**. You research and return a structured, citation-backed report as your final message. You must NOT write or edit any repo files — the report is your only output.

## Festivals to research
1. **Winnipeg Comedy Festival** (Apr 20–26 2026, winnipegcomedyfestival.com) — long-running; CBC TV gala tapings — how does TV production shape it?
2. **Halifax ComedyFest** (May 5–9, halifaxcomedyfest.ca) — likewise CBC-linked.
3. **Grindstone Comedy Festival** (July 2–12, Edmonton, grindstonecomedyfest.com) — 10 days; venue-run (Grindstone Theatre)? scale?
4. **Toronto Sketch Comedy Festival** (Mar 4–15, torontosketchfest.com) and **WHAT THE FESTIVAL!** (Sept 24–27, Toronto, wtfestival.ca) — brief; note Toronto also hosts JFL Toronto (researched by another agent).
5. **Great Outdoors Comedy Festival** (Aug 28–30 Vancouver stop, greatoutdoorscomedyfestival.com) — IMPORTANT STRUCTURAL CASE: it appears to be a TOURING outdoor amphitheatre series hitting multiple cities (Edmonton, Calgary, Winnipeg, Vancouver, US cities?). If so it is literally a music-festival-shaped comedy product (few stages, one show per act, roving cities) — the perfect contrast case for our taxonomy. Establish: how many cities/dates in 2026, stage count, ticketing (Ticketmaster? own?), operator (Trixstar?).
6. **Dubai Comedy Festival** (Oct 9–18, dubaicomedyfest.ae) — government-backed (Dubai Calendar / Brand Dubai?); scale; venues (Coca-Cola Arena + theatres?); one-night international acts model; ticketing (Platinumlist? Dubai Calendar?).
7. **Tokyo International Comedy Festival** (Sept 17–27, tokyocomedybar.com/festival) — run by Tokyo Comedy Bar? English-language standup scene; scale; brief.
8. **Lucille Ball Comedy Festival** (Aug 6–9, Jamestown NY, comedycenter.org/festival) — run by the National Comedy Center (a museum/institution) — the institution-anchored model; brief.

## Per-festival dossier fields (collect ALL; write NOT FOUND where you can't)
- **Organizer**: entity type (venue/nonprofit/promoter/government/broadcaster); stability; years running.
- **Recurrence**: annual? same city/venues? since when? For Great Outdoors: the roving pattern is the finding — document the city list instead.
- **Scale**: shows / venues / days; attendance if published.
- **Show model**: one-night showcases/galas vs repeated runs; curated vs submissions.
- **Venue geography**: count; walkable vs spread; for arena/outdoor events, capacity.
- **Clash reality**: parallel shows at peak — real scheduling problem or lineup-picking?
- **Ticketing**: central vs per-venue; vendor from purchase URLs (Ticketmaster/Eventbrite/Showpass/Platinumlist/…).
- **Data reachability**: fetch the schedule/lineup page with curl; server-rendered vs API-driven; concrete endpoints if visible. Don't build a scraper.
- **Concurrent festivals**: anything overlapping in the same city (e.g. Dubai October = ?, Winnipeg April = ?).
- **Official planner/app** if any.

## Method
- Outbound HTTPS works through a pre-configured proxy: `curl -sS -m 30 <url>` works for most sites. Fetch official pages (lineup/schedule, FAQ/ticketing). Preferred evidence.
- WebSearch for press and figures (CBC, local press, Chortle). Attribute figures to origin publishers.
- EVERY claim carries its source URL inline. Mark fetched vs snippet evidence. NOT FOUND is honest. Never invent.

## Output format
Final message = full report, markdown, dossier per festival, each bullet cited. One-line "fringe-like ↔ showcase-like" verdict per festival. End with all source URLs. Under ~300 lines.

Statement from Big Difference Company 
Big Difference Company, the charity that organised Leicester Comedy Festival, has become insolvent and ceased trading. This means the organisation is no longer operating and FRP Advisory Ltd are now dealing with the liquidation. 
The charity recognises the strength of feeling and frustration, particularly for those who are owed money.  
How was the charity funded?
The charity funded activities through three types of income:
Revenue generated by the charity's own activities during the Festival, such as Leicester Comedian of the Year, the UK Pun Championships and children's comedy events.
Revenue generated through charitable activities and events outside the Festival 
Grants, donations and sponsorship, including significant support from Leicester City Council, De Montfort University and other supporters over many years.
Together these income streams helped bridge the gap between the cost of delivering the Festival and the income generated directly by the Festival.
What has happened?
 For many years the Leicester Comedy Festival did not generate sufficient income for the charity to cover the full costs of planning, managing and delivering it. The charity therefore relied on the combination above  of fundraising, charitable activities, grants and donations to bridge that gap each year.
The charity provides the infrastructure that underpins the Festival, including year-round planning, administration, marketing, promotion, sponsorship, audience development, artist support, digital platforms and event management. Much of this work takes place throughout the year and many of the associated costs, particularly staffing costs, are fixed.
In recent years and months, the charity (like many others) experienced rising costs across almost every aspect of its operation, including salaries, National Insurance contributions, professional services, marketing, utilities and general operating costs whilst levels of grants, donations and sponsorship remained the same.
At the same time, income generated by the charity's activities reduced and grant funding did not increase or ceased. In real terms, this meant that the charity had fewer resources available despite continuing to deliver the Festival. 
The wider challenges facing charities, hospitality and the live comedy sector, including the impact of Covid-19 and the cost of living crisis, added further pressure.
Ultimately, the gap between income and expenditure became too large to bridge.
The charity took the necessary steps, including reporting to the Charity Commission and explored every avenue possible for support, including seeking to secure funding to enable the charity to survive. Ultimately that did not prove possible.

input.prompt:
You are a research agent for a product-wiki pass. Your territory: **(A) comedy-festival trackers/directories and (B) festival-planner tools beyond Edinburgh**. You research and return a structured, citation-backed report as your final message. You must NOT write or edit any repo files — the report is your only output.

Context: we build EdFringeNow (edfringenow.com), an Edinburgh Fringe discovery + trip-planning site, and are researching expansion into "help people plan any festival". Our wiki already profiles the Edinburgh-only planner competitors (Plan My Fringe, FringePlan, edfringeplanner.co.uk, Plan Your Fringe, Fringe Finder, Data Thistle etc.) — do NOT re-research those.

## Part A — festival trackers & directories
Sources that track/list many comedy festivals (the kind of thing we'd use to keep a festival calendar current). For each: who runs it, what it covers, how current it is, whether it's machine-readable.
1. **fromthecomicscomic.com/comedy-festivals/** — our seed. Who is behind From The Comic's Comic (Sean L. McCarthy?), how is the list maintained?
2. **Chortle** (chortle.co.uk) — the UK comedy trade site; does it keep a festival calendar/listings? What's at chortle.co.uk for festivals (try /festivals, look at their navigation)?
3. **British Comedy Guide** (comedy.co.uk) — festival directory?
4. **Wikipedia's list of comedy festivals** — how complete/current?
5. **World Fringe** (worldfringe.com) — the fringe-network directory (our wiki knows of it; check what its directory actually offers per festival: dates? links? data?).
6. Any others you find: comedy-festival submission platforms (FilmFreeway lists comedy festivals for performer submissions! — check what coverage looks like), festival-listing aggregators (everfest? festivalnet? musicfestivalwizard's comedy section?), punchup.live's role, dontstayin… whatever actually exists. Quality over quantity — 3-6 genuinely useful trackers beats 15 dead links.

## Part B — festival planner tools beyond Edinburgh
The question: does the "festival planner" product category exist outside Edinburgh, and what shape does it take?
1. **Per-festival planners**: search for third-party planner/scheduler tools for: Melbourne International Comedy Festival, Adelaide Fringe, Brighton Fringe, Just For Laughs Montreal, SXSW, Netflix Is A Joke, SF Sketchfest. (e.g. "MICF planner app", "Adelaide Fringe planner", "SXSW schedule builder third party".) Report what exists and what doesn't — a well-verified "nothing exists for X" is a valuable finding.
2. **Official apps as planners**: which major festivals ship official apps with itinerary/favourites features (Adelaide Fringe app? MICF app? SXSW GO?) — one line each.
3. **Music-festival planner category**: the structural analogue. **Clashfinders** (clashfinder.com — user-maintained lineup grids for hundreds of music festivals), **Woov**, **Festival Scout**, lineup-tracking apps (**Lineupning**?), **Rate Your Music/Songkick festival tools**? For each real one: what it does, coverage, who runs it, business model. Clashfinder especially: it's the closest thing to a generic "festival schedule clash" tool — how does it get its data (crowdsourced?), does it cover comedy/fringe festivals at all?
4. **Generic trip/event planners** that market festival planning (TripIt-for-festivals type products, Fever/DICE discovery apps' festival features) — only if genuinely relevant, one line each.

## Method
- Outbound HTTPS works through a pre-configured proxy: `curl -sS -m 30 <url>` works for most sites — fetch pages (e.g. clashfinder.com, chortle.co.uk, worldfringe.com directory pages) and read them. Preferred evidence.
- WebSearch to discover tools and for anything a fetch can't answer. Attribute claims to origin publishers.
- EVERY claim carries its source URL inline. Mark fetched vs snippet evidence. "Nothing found" with the searches you ran listed is a GOOD answer for Part B items. Never invent.

## Output format
Final message = full report, markdown. Part A: one dossier per tracker (who runs, coverage, currency, machine-readability, URL). Part B: per-festival planner findings (exists/doesn't, evidence), official apps list, music-festival planner dossiers. End with all source URLs used. Under ~300 lines.

- WebSearch to discover tools and for anything a fetch can't answer. Attribute claims to origin publishers.
- EVERY claim carries its source URL inline. Mark fetched vs snippet evidence. "Nothing found" with the searches you ran listed is a GOOD answer for Part B items. Never invent.

Final message = full report, markdown. Part A: one dossier per tracker (who runs, coverage, currency, machine-readability, URL). Part B: per-festival planner findings (exists/doesn't, evidence), official apps list, music-festival planner dossiers. End with all source URLs used. Under ~300 lines.

 April 20-26,2026 | Winnipeg Comedy Festival Skip to Navigation Skip to Content Skip to Footer Join us April 26 - May 2, 2027 Home Shows Alumni About Us News Shop Search Search News April 20-26,2026 Apr 20, 2026 WCF launches its 25th anniversary today with many shows already sold-out! 30+ shows. 9 venues. 85 comics. One city.     FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE Winnipeg, April 20, 2026 – The Winnipeg Comedy Festival (WCF) , presented by Manitoba Liquor Mart , officially launches today, beginning seven days of laughter, live performances, nationally broadcast tapings, and suspiciously high spirits across the city. Now celebrating its 25th anniversary , WCF runs April 20 to 26 with more than 30 shows across 9 venues , featuring 85 comics from Winnipeg and across Canada. What began here in Winnipeg has grown into one of Canada’s most-watched comedy festival broadcasts, thanks in no small part to loyal local audiences. This milestone year starts off with seven shows already sold-out, and nine more on low-ticket warning. The 25th anniversary also features five recorded-for-broadcast Mega Shows at the Burton Cummings Theatre, a special Debaters joint-anniversary celebration, intimate performances at the Gas Station Arts Centre, special events throughout the city, and ample proof that comedy remains an excellent civic resource. Artistic Director Dean Jenkinson says, “Our Mega Shows at the Burton Cummings Theatre are an exceptionally strong curation of Canadian comedy talent, combining old friends of the festival with many exciting new faces, all gathered to bring the funny and celebrate, well, us. For our 25th anniversary, we wanted lineups worthy of the occasion, and I think audiences are going to see exactly that.” THE MEGA SHOWS Burton Cummings Theatre | 364 Smith Street My Best Life Thursday, April 23, 7:30pm Hosted by Brooke Lynn Hytes (Canada's Drag Race) New to Town Friday, April 24, 6:30pm Hosted by Dave Merheje (Mr. D) 25th Anniversary Gala Friday, April 24, 9:15pm Hosted by Shaun Majumder (22 Minutes, 24) Chip Off the Old Block Saturday, April 25, 6:30pm Hosted by Chris Wilson (22 Minutes) You Had to Be There Saturday, April 25, 9:15pm Hosted by Jann Arden (Canada's sweetheart singer-songwriter-storyteller) Five live television tapings. One very lucky audience. Executive Director Nick Kowalchuk says: “I love this time of year because we get to welcome old friends and brand-new ones into the Winnipeg Comedy Festival’s home at the Gas Station Arts Centre. It’s where audiences can catch edgy, experimental, and exciting comedy every night. We've already sold out many shows, but there's still lots of fabulous options!” JUST SOME OF THOSE FABULOUS OPTIONS INCLUDE: You Talk Funny: Comedy Conversations with Brad Oswald Wednesday, April 22 to Friday, April 24 11:00am & 12:00pm, Fairmont Winnipeg Lobby Former Winnipeg Free Press entertainment reporter Brad Oswald is coaxed out of retirement to host candid conversations with festival favourites. Pop in, sit down, and enjoy stories, laughs, and expertly deployed questions. Featuring guests from across the festival lineup, including veteran favourites, first-time performers, and the occasional charming surprise. Check out the website for full details!  FAQs | Winnipeg Comedy Festival Skip to Navigation Skip to Content Skip to Footer Join us April 26 - May 2, 2027 Home Shows Alumni About Us News Shop Search Search FAQs Frequently Asked Questions Ticketing What is 3Common? 3Common is a Winnipeg-based ticketing service that we use for all shows not held at Ticketmaster-contracted venues. By using 3Common, we support local while keeping online ticket fees lower for you. Win-win! Why does WCF use Ticketmaster? Some venues have exclusive contracts with Ticketmaster, meaning we must use their system when we rent those spaces. Our Mega Shows require a large venue for cameras, cast, crew, and production equipment, and Burton Cummings Theatre is one of the only venues that fits those needs. Plus, it’s a beautiful piece of Winnipeg history! My discount code isn’t working—why not? Make sure you click “unlock” on the right-hand side of the purchase page before entering your code. That usually fixes the issue! If you still have trouble, contact us at (204) 284-9477 or tickets@winnipegcomedyfestival.com . Programming Which shows are child-friendly? The Winnipeg Comedy Festival was founded in 2002 by Lara Rae and CBC Radio’s Tom Anniko in partnership with the Gas Station Arts Centre (GSAC). What began as a single festival has grown into GSAC’s flagship event, featuring year-round outreach programs, rural tours, workshops, and acclaimed television broadcasts. Today, WCF continues to showcase Canada’s top comedic talent while fostering emerging voices, drawing audiences from across the country. With over 2 million viewers tuning in annually, WCF remains CBC Television’s highest-rated comedy festival series—proof that Winnipeg knows how to bring the laughs, both on stage and on screen. ## Summary

The Big Difference Company, which runs the Leicester Comedy Festival, has gone bust and announced it had "become insolvent and ceased trading," leaving hundreds of comedians owed money for performing there likely to go unpaid.

## Key Details

**Financial Impact:**
- The company collapsed with debts of at least £215,000, with an initial creditors' report showing the Big Difference Company went into liquidation owing more than 100 people money.
- This includes six staff members owed more than £50,000 between them.

**Background:**
- Chortle first reported the company was in financial difficulties back in April, and it submitted a 'serious incident report' to the Charity Commission after a venue it operated was repossessed over unpaid rent.

**Aftermath:**
- A new festival called The Independent Comedy Festival is being put together by comedians and promoters owed money by Big Difference Company, taking place at the same time in February, with a business model that ensures comedians get paid.

import re, html
def textof(f, n=3000):
    t = open(f, encoding='utf-8', errors='replace').read()
    t2 = re.sub(r'<(script|style)[^>]*>.*?</\1>', ' ', t, flags=re.S|re.I)
    text = re.sub(r'<[^>]+>', ' ', t2)
    return html.unescape(re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', text))[:n], t
for f in ['sketchfest.html','wtf.html','grindstone.html']:
    tx, raw = textof(f)
    print(f"===== {f} ({len(raw)} bytes) =====")
    print(tx)
    print("----- interesting links -----")
    links = sorted(set(re.findall(r'href="([^"]+)"', raw)))
    keep = [l for l in links if re.search(r'(show|event|ticket|schedul|lineup|about|festival|pass|faq|apply|submi)', l, re.I) and not re.search(r'\.(css|js|png|jpg|svg|ico)', l)]
    for l in keep[:40]: print(l)
    print()
EOF

===== chortle-bust.html =====
Leicester Comedy Festival firm goes bust : News 2026 :     Chortle : The UK Comedy Guide
South East  -  Hants, Dorset and Wiltshire
Insolvent Big Difference Company ceases trading
The company that runs the Leicester Comedy Festival has gone bust – meaning the hundreds of comedians owed money for performing there are likely to go unpaid.
The Big Difference Company has announced ‘with great sadness’ that it had ‘become insolvent and ceased trading’.
The news is not entirely unexpected, but will still come as a blow to performers owed their ticket money from February’s event.  Chortle was the first to report that the company was in financial difficulties
– and last month it submitted a ‘serious incident report’ to the Charity Commission, after the venue it also operates was repossessed over unpaid rent.
In a statement sent to the BBC, the company said: ‘For 32 years, [the festival] has been an important part of the cultural and economic life of our region, showcasing comedy talent, attracting visitors, and supporting local businesses and venues.
‘We acknowledge that this news will be deeply disappointing to staff, performers, venues, promoters and supporters. We recognise the significant impact this will have on our employees, performers, venues, suppliers and other creditors, and we are sincerely sorry to all those affected.'
The directors said they ‘worked tirelessly to avoid this outcome’,  but said it was ‘not possible to secure a sustainable future’.
But they added that their financial problems may not be the end of the line for the festival – the biggest of its kind – saying they planned to ‘explore how a sustainable long-term future can be secured for this much-loved festival’.
Reacting to the news, Jessica Toomey, director of the 1,600-member Live Comedy Association, said: ‘We are incredibly sad about the dreadful impact this will have on many of our members and the wider live comedy sector across the UK.
‘Leicester Comedy Festival has been a beacon of UK live comedy each February since 1994 and has helped develop the careers of many comedians, as well as supporting promoters, venues and the wider comedy community.  Our thoughts are with those people who are still owed money, some of them a considerable amount.’
‘ We also hope that a new festival can emerge from the ashes and help sustain the legacy built up over more than 30 years.’
Michael Day, from the variety branch of performers' union Equity added: 'Despite being widely anticipated, it’s a huge blow to see Leicester Comedy Festival file for insolvency.
'The festival has been a huge feature on the comedy calendar for many years, being the largest comedy-only performance festival and providing hundreds of gigs to both seasoned stand-ups and those seeking to break into the comedy scene. It’s terrible news and leaves many performers unpaid from this year’s festival.
'At Equity, we’ve been supporting many comedians who were left unpaid and we have secured payment for several of them. However, getting money owed to comedians will become far more difficult under an insolvency.'
He also called for more protection for performer regarding unpaid fees, adding: 'There would be no festival or gigs without these comedians and it’s grossly unfair that they are the ones left unpaid in this and so many similar situations.'
The Live Comedy Association yesterday launched a
to try to secure £30,000 to support acts, promoters and others  affected by the Big Difference Company’s woes.  It follows the £5,000 which was distributed by the LCA last month.
Anthony Lamb, the former manager of The Big Difference venue, has raised more than £20,000 from a separate
to reopen the building under the name Forum Porcorum.

===== chortle-newfest.html =====
Leicester gets a new comedy festival : News 2026 :     Chortle : The UK Comedy Guide
South East  -  Hants, Dorset and Wiltshire
...and this one vows to pay its comedians
A new festival is to emerge from the ashes of the collapsed Leicester Comedy Festival.
The project is being put together by some of the comedians and promoters owed money by the previous organisers, The Big Difference Company, which went into insolvency this month.
Called The Independent Comedy Festival, it will take place at the same time of year, February, and will again feature hundreds of shows in many of the same venues.
And they have promised a business model that ensures comedians get paid.
, pictured, who lives in Leicester and is compere at many of the city’s established venues.
He said: ‘We’re going to put on something really special. Leicester deserves a brilliant comedy festival, artists deserve to be treated fairly, and audiences should know that their ticket money is going to support the show they have paid to see.
‘For too long in the comedy industry, comedians have been at the bottom of the pecking order. It’s time to start again. Hopefully comedians can trust that with one of their own kind at the helm, The Independent Comedy Festival will treat artists with the respect they deserve.
He added that the festival will be ‘run responsibly by people from the industry who will give the festival the love that it needs’.
Hylton founded the festival with Colin Bowles, who puts on shows at several venues across Leicester through his company TripleCeePee. He vowed the event would ‘continue the legacy’ established by the previous festival.
Mark Watson, who also runs production company Impatient, said he would be supporting the new venture.  He said:  ‘Leicester as a city has supported a unique, hugely valuable festival for many years now, and [the collapse of Big Difference] would leave a huge gap in the comedy calendar.
‘I'm very happy to hear that that gap is going to be filled by people who know what they're doing and truly care about comedy. I'm excited to see what comes next, and look forward to being part of it for years to come, unless I stop being funny.’
Leicester City Council – one of the main partners of the collapsed festival – previously vowed to do what it could help maintain a comedy event in the city.
Hundreds of comedians, producers and promoters owed money for performing at this year’s festival are likely to go unpaid after  The Big Difference Company  – a registered charity – declared itself insolvent and ceased trading.  Venue operator Just The Tonic have said they are owed more than £13,000 in ticket sales only from the collapse.
The Independent Comedy Festival will be working with ticket platform TixEvery, which would pay comedians directly, with the festival having no access to box office receipts.
‘Artists can trust that their ticket revenue will be kept secure,’ Hylton said.
And speaking of which comedians might be coming to the city in February, he said: ‘We’ve got some amazing acts signed up already, I’m so excited for people to see what we’ve got up our sleeve when we announce the lineup later this year.’
News of the new festival has been welcomed by The Live Comedy Association, with chair Jessica Toomey saying: ‘The city has a massive reputation for supporting live comedy and we wish the producers of the new festival all the best. We hope many of our members will get behind the new festival to help ensure it’s a massive celebration of UK comedy.’
Hylton added that he was looking to work with the local authority, businesses, venues ‘and anybody else who believes they can help.’

content.content: Netflix Is A Joke Festival 2026 Schedule Artists Venues Featured Shows Frequently Asked Questions Lineups are subject to change. Performers, guests, and show elements may be added, removed, or substituted without notice. No refunds or exchanges will be issued due to changes in the lineup. All door times and show times are subject to change. Please refer to your ticketing page for the most up-to-date information prior to arrival, as times may be adjusted at any time. Is there a lost & found? Where is it? If you lose something, please check in with the venue you think you lost it at and they will be able to check their lost & found. A list of venues can be found here . What does the Ticketmaster Platinum ticket mean? Why do you have it? Official Platinum Seats are premium tickets made available by artists and event providers through Ticketmaster that give fans fair and safe access to some of the best seats in the house. For more info, visit the FAQ. Is the festival okay for kids? We would call the festival 18+ as most of the shows skew towards a more mature audience. Some of the venues are a strict 21+ so please double check on the ticket page before you purchase. I don’t see tickets for a performer on the lineup I want to see, are they playing the festival? Ticket and venue information for certain performances will be updated at a later date. Be sure to subscribe to our mailing list below for updates from Netflix is a Joke Fest. Can I leave a show in the middle of the performance? It’s kind of rude to leave in the middle of an amazing show that you paid your hard earned cash for, but if something comes up, sure, you can go. Just try to be quiet when you do. For recorded performances, we kindly ask you to stay seated for the duration of the show, so please plan your trip to the restroom accordingly. Might I be filmed? Some shows are being recorded, some are not. We always recommend looking your best. Check each specific show page for more information. I bought tickets but can no longer go to the show. Can I exchange them? The ability to sell or exchange your tickets will vary from event to event. But if you find yourself unable to attend, you can take advantage of Ticketmaster’s Ticket Transfer feature. It’s a safe and simple way to send tickets to friends or family right from your Ticketmaster account. From your account, view your ticket order and tap the Transfer Tickets button to get started. Please note: some events may not have Ticket Transfer available. Check your ticket details in your Ticketmaster account for eligibility. Is there a dress code and can I dress up? Just the basics. No shirt, no shoes, no comedy. And if you’re attending one of the live recordings it’s best to avoid wearing loud colors, patterns, logos or hats. They don’t look as good on TV. Trust us. Also, these shows are very time sensitive so please arrive at least a half hour before the show time because your seat could be subject to change after the show has started. Are these shows ADA accessible? Yes. All venues that are part of the festival are ADA compliant. Please visit individual venue websites for the specifics. What’s security like? Everyone entering will need to go through a bag check, metal detectors and general security. Leave the nunchucks at home! Do I need a ticket? Yes. You need tickets. For every show you want to go to, you’ll need an individual ticket. There are no festival passes that grant you access to every event. Making your own lanyard is strictly a fashion choice. What’s the cellphone policy? Can I take photos or videos at the performances? Most shows will allow you to take your phone in the venue, but you must keep it off during performances. In general, you may not record or photograph any of the performances at any time. Failure to adhere may result in expulsion. Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding the Leicester Comedy Festival's recent funding crisis:

## Recent Financial Crisis

Following the 2026 Leicester Comedy Festival, hundreds of comedians remained unpaid and the festival faced significant backlash for failing to pay performers. The producers of the festival (registered charity Big Difference Company) announced they were unable to pay comedians and promoters ticket money from shows.

## Causes and Response

Organisers cited temporary cashflow problems caused by delays in receiving funding from sponsors and third-party ticket sales. The majority of ticket monies had not been sent to acts or promoters, and Big Difference Company submitted a serious incident report to the Charity Commission over its ongoing financial issues.

## Support Initiatives

The Live Comedy Association (LCA) launched a fundraising campaign to support affected acts and promoters, with an initial target of £30,000. Additionally, the Live Comedy Association noted that grassroots live comedy receives far less support than other live arts, and without investment in emerging talent and supporting independent venues, the UK risks losing diverse, original voices.

The search results indicate this has been a significant crisis for the UK comedy sector, with broader implications for how comedy funding is prioritized compared to other cultural industries.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about the Melbourne International Comedy Festival 2026 and its app features:

The Festival's website and app have streamlined navigation of shows with minimal inputs, utilizing user testing to present useful filters and show options, aided by smart auto-suggestions for search terms.

When users find a show that interests them, they can view all performance dates and times including ticket discounts and preview shows, and a quick tap adds it to their favourites list - this combined list can then be used to buy multiple tickets in a combined transaction on Ticketmaster.

There are over 750 shows on offer at the 2026 Festival, with options ranging from comedy legends, rising stars, international icons and family fun. The Melbourne International Comedy Festival returns from 25 March to 19 April 2026.

General
Are there any age restrictions?
** Canada shows only **
These events are all NO MINORS (18+ or 19+, depending on the province) – no exceptions. This includes infants.
What are the set times?
Check your show’s individual city page for the schedule. Exact comedian stage times will not be posted as the schedule is subject to change. Make sure to come down early – the festivities start as soon as you walk in!
Are there any live stream ticket options available?
No – everything is live and in person.
What food and amenities are at the festival?
The festival site is fully licensed! Both alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages will be available for purchase, as well as various food options including choices for those with dietary restrictions.
What forms of ID are acceptable?
Any official and unexpired government-issued driver’s license or ID card containing a photograph and date of birth.
Any official and unexpired government-issued passport containing a photograph and date of birth.
Any official temporary license proving you are currently renewing a license – ONLY if accompanied by the expired driver’s license.
The following forms of identification will not be accepted for access to the grounds: school ID, consular ID, birth certificates, expired IDs of any kind (unless specifically mentioned otherwise), and photos of IDs
I'm a comedian. How can I perform at the festival?
Unfortunately, we are not an open submissions event and we do not have an application process to be considered.
How do I apply to volunteer, bartend or be a vendor at the festival?

page here to learn more and apply!
Festival rules
What should I bring?
Government issued photo identification
A jacket or blanket for the cooler evenings
A charged up phone!
Credit card or debit card

Festival approved camping chair - See chair info below this FAQ (VIP tables, VIP Club come with chairs)

Umbrellas under 42″ in diameter (cannot have metal or pointed tips)

What should I leave at home?
No outside drinks are permitted (only up to 1L of water in a factory sealed bottle)
No home made food permitted (commercially sealed snacks only)
Your kids who are under the legal age! (no minors)
Glass containers or glass of any kind
Hard-sided coolers or wagons
Chairs that do not collapse, two-person chairs, couches, etc
