# City context sources — finding everything else that's on

Where "what else is going on in this city" gets published, and how a product
can read it. This page exists on the owner's direction (2026-09-01): a
festival visitor also wants the rest of the city — other events that week,
attractions, markets — and the wiki's job is **not** to hold any particular
weekend's events but to hold **the sources**: which publications, feeds and
APIs carry a city's non-festival goings-on, per festival city, and how
machine-readable each is. Scoped to the cities of the longer festivals
([comedy-festival-circuit/](../comedy-festival-circuit/README.md)'s
fringe-shaped tier), not the weekend showcases. Edinburgh's own August
*festival* cluster is [festival-season/](../festival-season/README.md)'s;
this page is about everything those pages don't list. Compiled once, refined
in place.

Every claim below was verified by direct fetch on 2026-09-01 unless marked
as a search-attributed claim; "closed" verdicts name what was actually
probed.

## Key insights

- Events listings are a per-country licensed market: Data Thistle (UK), ATDW (Australia), Eventfinda (NZ) cover our cities in one API each.
- Montreal is the outlier: the city's own open-data portal publishes its events calendar as CSV/GeoJSON, refreshed daily.
- Tourism-board sites have no APIs — but their event detail pages carry schema.org JSON-LD, so one parser covers every city.
- The open-API era is over: Eventbrite killed public event search in 2020, Songkick takes no new keys, Fever bought DICE.
- Ticketmaster Discovery and Skiddle are the free keyed baseline — geo-searchable, 5k calls/day, with a ticketed-music skew.
- Attractions are solved free: OSM Overpass plus Wikidata; Viator's no-gate affiliate tier adds bookable tours with commission.
- Data Thistle is competitor and supplier at once: it sells the listings feed the UK's own tourism boards run on.

## The source classes

**1. Tourism-board (DMO) event calendars** are the best human-curated
coverage of "everything else in town" — promoters submit events directly
(every DMO probed has a submit flow) — and the weakest machine surface: none
probed offers a documented API. The verified pattern across seven DMOs:
index pages carry only site-level JSON-LD, but **event detail pages carry
full schema.org `Event` markup** (wellingtonnz.com's detail pages have
`MusicEvent` with `startDate` and `Place`), so the generic integration is a
sitemap crawl plus a JSON-LD parse of detail pages — one parser for every
city. Some have undocumented JSON backends (aucklandnz.com calls its own
`/api/events/get`); some are bot-hostile (visitmelbourne.com 403s
non-browsers; What's On Melbourne renders client-side).

**2. City open-data portals** carry attractions/POI and event
*infrastructure*, not live listings — with one exception worth building on:
[Montreal's "Événements publics" dataset](https://donnees.montreal.ca/)
(CKAN, API works unauthenticated) is the city's own calendar as
CSV/GeoJSON — date, event type, audience, cost, location — last modified
the day it was checked, i.e. maintained daily. Melbourne's Opendatasoft
portal (239 datasets, open API) has venues, landmarks and event *permits*
but no calendar; Edinburgh's legacy portal was unreachable (502) and its
live ArcGIS portal is spatial-only.

**3. Commercial listings media** (Time Out, The Skinny, Broadsheet, The
List's consumer site) are editorial and scrape-only; no licensing program
surfaced for Time Out. The class that matters sits behind them:

**4. Licensed events-data suppliers — the class the UK actually runs on.**
[Data Thistle](https://www.datathistle.com/) (The List's data arm,
Edinburgh-based) claims over half a million future performances UK-wide and
publishes a [documented Publishing API](https://api.datathistle.com/) —
free registration, event/place/schedule/performance model **with
per-performance prices and booking links** — and its named clients include
VisitScotland, Visit Brighton, Visit Liverpool and Transport for Edinburgh,
via the Simpleview CMS the DMOs run on. One integration would cover
Edinburgh, Brighton and Leicester at once — and its data model is
structurally a superset of what EdFringeNow already stores. Australia's
equivalent is national and official: the
[Australian Tourism Data Warehouse ATLAS API](https://developer.atdw.com.au/)
(products *and events*, feeding the state DMO sites; distributor
registration A$660 once-off with a 30-day trial, per its own FAQ) — one
paid integration covers Melbourne and Adelaide. New Zealand's is
[Eventfinda's API](https://www.eventfinda.co.nz/api/v2/index) (free key by
application, display-only licence with attribution) covering Auckland and
Wellington.

**5. Ticketing-platform discovery APIs** — the survivors and the dead:
[Ticketmaster Discovery](https://developer.ticketmaster.com/products-and-docs/apis/discovery-api/v2/)
(free key, 5,000 calls/day, geo+date+venue search, global) and
[Skiddle](https://github.com/Skiddle/web-api) (UK; free key, lat/long/radius,
event codes including COMEDY and EXHIB) are real and open.
**Eventbrite has no public discovery API** — the public event search was
removed in February 2020 and the API is org-scoped now; **Songkick** takes
no new API applications (commercial licence ~$500/month per its support
pages); **DICE** is partner-only and was acquired by **Fever** (itself
closed) in June 2025; **Bandsintown** is artist-scoped — the wrong shape
for city-wide discovery. Universe has an open GraphQL API but niche
inventory.

**6. Event-intelligence aggregators**: [PredictHQ](https://docs.predicthq.com/)
sells exactly "all events in a city" (free tier exists; real pricing
negotiated) but is built for demand forecasting — whether its licence
permits consumer republishing is unverified and decides whether it is
usable at all. SeatGeek's Platform API is real, free-keyed, US-leaning.

**7. Attractions, as distinct from events**: the free, licence-clean base
layer is [OpenStreetMap's Overpass API](https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Overpass_API)
(`tourism=attraction|museum|viewpoint`, opening hours where mapped) joined
with [Wikidata's SPARQL endpoint](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:SPARQL_query_service)
(CC0 entities, coordinates, images, Wikipedia links) — the "free hour near
me" gazetteer, and the machine version of the hand-curated list
[festival-season/](../festival-season/README.md) said couldn't exist as a
feed. For *bookable* attractions,
[Viator's Partner API basic-access tier is free with no pre-authorization](https://docs.viator.com/partner-api/technical/)
(search, availability, pricing, commission on referred bookings) — which
also plugs into the affiliate lane
[competitor-landscape/](../competitor-landscape/README.md)'s revenue
analysis found empty among rivals; GetYourGuide gates its API behind 100k
monthly visits and Tiqets behind partner contact; Google Places is paid
per-request; Atlas Obscura is bot-blocked with no API.

## Per-city: what a product would actually read

| City (festival, window) | Best sources | Machine access |
|---|---|---|
| Edinburgh (Fringe, Aug) | Data Thistle API; The List editorial; Ticketmaster + Skiddle | documented API; scrape; APIs |
| Melbourne (MICF, Mar–Apr) | ATDW ATLAS API; What's On Melbourne; data.melbourne | paid API; headless scrape only; open API (POI, no listings) |
| Adelaide (Fringe, Feb–Mar) | ATDW (same integration); southaustralia.com (ATDW-powered) | paid API; detail-page scrape |
| Brighton (Fringe, May) | Data Thistle (VisitBrighton is its client); visitbrighton.com | same UK API; JSON-LD scrape |
| Montreal (JFL, Jul) | city open-data events dataset; mtl.org; Ticketmaster | CSV/GeoJSON, daily; JS site; API |
| Auckland + Wellington (NZICF, May) | Eventfinda API; DMO sites | free key + attribution; JSON-LD scrape |
| Leicester (comedy festival, Feb) | Data Thistle; visitleicester.info; Skiddle | same UK API; detail-page scrape; API |

The synthesis the research supports: **three integrations cover the need at
lowest cost** — (1) one licensed listings API per country (Data Thistle /
ATDW / Eventfinda, with Montreal's open data replacing the class there),
(2) Ticketmaster Discovery + Skiddle as the free cross-city baseline, and
(3) OSM + Wikidata for attractions with Viator's affiliate tier when
bookable tours (and their commission) are wanted. The universal fallback
for any DMO without an API is the sitemap-crawl + `Event` JSON-LD parse.
Time Out, Eventbrite, Songkick, Fever/DICE and Atlas Obscura are closed for
this purpose and not worth integration effort.

## Sources

- [Data Thistle](https://www.datathistle.com/) and the [Publishing API](https://api.datathistle.com/) — coverage claim, client list, data model with per-performance prices; fetched 2026-09-01.
- [ATDW — distributor registration and FAQ](https://atdw.com.au/) and the [ATLAS API documentation](https://developer.atdw.com.au/) — the A$660 registration and 30-day trial are ATDW's own stated terms.
- [Eventfinda API](https://www.eventfinda.co.nz/api/v2/index) and [its terms](https://www.eventfinda.co.nz/api/terms) — free key, display-only licence, attribution.
- [Ville de Montréal open data — package search](https://donnees.montreal.ca/) — the "Événements publics" dataset (CSV/GeoJSON/SHP), modified same-day at check.
- [Ticketmaster Discovery API](https://developer.ticketmaster.com/products-and-docs/apis/discovery-api/v2/) — free key, 5,000 calls/day, 5 req/sec defaults.
- [Skiddle web API (GitHub)](https://github.com/Skiddle/web-api) — free key by application; event codes including COMEDY and EXHIB.
- [Eventbrite platform docs](https://www.eventbrite.com/platform/docs/introduction) and the [public-search removal record (Automattic's eventbrite-api issue)](https://github.com/Automattic/eventbrite-api/issues/83) — no public discovery endpoint since Feb 2020.
- [Songkick API support page](https://support.songkick.com/hc/en-us/articles/360012423194) — closed to new applications; commercial licence pricing as stated there.
- [DICE partners](https://dice.fm/partners) and [Fever's acquisition of DICE (Fever newsroom)](https://newsroom.feverup.com/) — partner-only API; June 2025 acquisition.
- [Bandsintown artist API docs](https://artists.bandsintown.com/support/api) — artist-scoped access.
- [PredictHQ docs](https://docs.predicthq.com/) and [pricing page](https://www.predicthq.com/pricing) — plans self-reported; republishing terms unverified.
- [Viator Partner API — levels of access](https://partnerresources.viator.com/travel-commerce/levels-of-access/) and [technical docs](https://docs.viator.com/partner-api/technical/) — free basic affiliate tier, no pre-authorization.
- [GetYourGuide partner API gate](https://partner.getyourguide.support/hc/en-us/articles/13981133907613) — ≥100k monthly visits for Basic.
- [Overpass API (OSM wiki)](https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Overpass_API) and [Wikidata SPARQL service](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:SPARQL_query_service).
- [Google Places web service](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/places/web-service/overview) — paid per-request; [Things to do is operator-side](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/13189190).
- DMO probes, all fetched 2026-09-01: [wellingtonnz.com events](https://www.wellingtonnz.com/visit/events) (detail-page `MusicEvent` JSON-LD), [aucklandnz.com events](https://www.aucklandnz.com/events) (internal `/api/events/get`), [What's On Melbourne](https://whatson.melbourne.vic.gov.au/) (client-rendered), [visitmelbourne.com](https://www.visitmelbourne.com/) (403 to non-browsers), [data.melbourne explore API](https://data.melbourne.vic.gov.au/), [southaustralia.com](https://southaustralia.com/) (ATDW asset URLs), [visitbrighton.com](https://www.visitbrighton.com/whats-on/) (Simpleview CMS), [visitleicester.info](https://www.visitleicester.info/whats-on/), [edinburgh.org what's-on](https://edinburgh.org/whats-on/), [mtl.org](https://www.mtl.org/en/what-to-do/festivals-and-events), [lavitrine.com](https://www.lavitrine.com/) (JS SPA, no public API), [timeout.com/edinburgh](https://www.timeout.com/edinburgh), [list.co.uk](https://list.co.uk/), [atlasobscura.com](https://www.atlasobscura.com/) (403).

## Open questions

- **What does Data Thistle actually cost, and would its licence allow our
  static-file architecture?** Registration is free but commercial licensing
  is contact-priced — the same two questions
  [festival-season/](../festival-season/README.md) has open against the
  Edinburgh Festivals Listings API (redistribution vs our committed-JSON
  model), now against the UK-wide supplier too. One conversation covers
  both of its roles (supplier here, competitor on
  [competitor-landscape/](../competitor-landscape/README.md)).
- **Does Data Thistle's feed carry the Fringe itself at scrape-grade
  fidelity?** If its half-million UK performances include the full Fringe
  programme with prices, it is also a candidate *second source* for our

- **PredictHQ's republishing terms** — unverified, and they decide whether

+# City context sources — finding everything else that's on
+
+Where "what else is going on in this city" gets published, and how a product
+can read it. This page exists on the owner's direction (2026-09-01): a
+festival visitor also wants the rest of the city — other events that week,
+attractions, markets — and the wiki's job is **not** to hold any particular
+weekend's events but to hold **the sources**: which publications, feeds and
+APIs carry a city's non-festival goings-on, per festival city, and how
+machine-readable each is. Scoped to the cities of the longer festivals
+([comedy-festival-circuit/](../comedy-festival-circuit/README.md)'s
+fringe-shaped tier), not the weekend showcases. Edinburgh's own August
+*festival* cluster is [festival-season/](../festival-season/README.md)'s;
+this page is about everything those pages don't list. Compiled once, refined
+in place.
+
+Every claim below was verified by direct fetch on 2026-09-01 unless marked
+as a search-attributed claim; "closed" verdicts name what was actually
+probed.
+
+## Key insights
+
+- Events listings are a per-country licensed market: Data Thistle (UK), ATDW (Australia), Eventfinda (NZ) cover our cities in one API each.
+- Montreal is the outlier: the city's own open-data portal publishes its events calendar as CSV/GeoJSON, refreshed daily.
+- Tourism-board sites have no APIs — but their event detail pages carry schema.org JSON-LD, so one parser covers every city.
+- The open-API era is over: Eventbrite killed public event search in 2020, Songkick takes no new keys, Fever bought DICE.
+- Ticketmaster Discovery and Skiddle are the free keyed baseline — geo-searchable, 5k calls/day, with a ticketed-music skew.
+- Attractions are solved free: OSM Overpass plus Wikidata; Viator's no-gate affiliate tier adds bookable tours with commission.
+- Data Thistle is competitor and supplier at once: it sells the listings feed the UK's own tourism boards run on.
+

+coverage of "everything else in town" — promoters submit events directly

+probed offers a documented API. The verified pattern across seven DMOs:
+index pages carry only site-level JSON-LD, but **event detail pages carry

+`MusicEvent` with `startDate` and `Place`), so the generic integration is a
+sitemap crawl plus a JSON-LD parse of detail pages — one parser for every

+`/api/events/get`); some are bot-hostile (visitmelbourne.com 403s
+non-browsers; What's On Melbourne renders client-side).

+**2. City open-data portals** carry attractions/POI and event
+*infrastructure*, not live listings — with one exception worth building on:
+[Montreal's "Événements publics" dataset](https://donnees.montreal.ca/)

+CSV/GeoJSON — date, event type, audience, cost, location — last modified

+portal (239 datasets, open API) has venues, landmarks and event *permits*
+but no calendar; Edinburgh's legacy portal was unreachable (502) and its
+live ArcGIS portal is spatial-only.
+
+**3. Commercial listings media** (Time Out, The Skinny, Broadsheet, The
+List's consumer site) are editorial and scrape-only; no licensing program
+surfaced for Time Out. The class that matters sits behind them:
+
+**4. Licensed events-data suppliers — the class the UK actually runs on.**
+[Data Thistle](https://www.datathistle.com/) (The List's data arm,
+Edinburgh-based) claims over half a million future performances UK-wide and
+publishes a [documented Publishing API](https://api.datathistle.com/) —
+free registration, event/place/schedule/performance model **with
+per-performance prices and booking links** — and its named clients include
+VisitScotland, Visit Brighton, Visit Liverpool and Transport for Edinburgh,
+via the Simpleview CMS the DMOs run on. One integration would cover
+Edinburgh, Brighton and Leicester at once — and its data model is
+structurally a superset of what EdFringeNow already stores. Australia's
+equivalent is national and official: the

+paid integration covers Melbourne and Adelaide. New Zealand's is
+[Eventfinda's API](https://www.eventfinda.co.nz/api/v2/index) (free key by
+application, display-only licence with attribution) covering Auckland and
+Wellington.
+
+**5. Ticketing-platform discovery APIs** — the survivors and the dead:
+[Ticketmaster Discovery](https://developer.ticketmaster.com/products-and-docs/apis/discovery-api/v2/)
+(free key, 5,000 calls/day, geo+date+venue search, global) and
+[Skiddle](https://github.com/Skiddle/web-api) (UK; free key, lat/long/radius,
+event codes including COMEDY and EXHIB) are real and open.
+**Eventbrite has no public discovery API** — the public event search was
+removed in February 2020 and the API is org-scoped now; **Songkick** takes
+no new API applications (commercial licence ~$500/month per its support
+pages); **DICE** is partner-only and was acquired by **Fever** (itself
+closed) in June 2025; **Bandsintown** is artist-scoped — the wrong shape
+for city-wide discovery. Universe has an open GraphQL API but niche
+inventory.
+
+**6. Event-intelligence aggregators**: [PredictHQ](https://docs.predicthq.com/)
+sells exactly "all events in a city" (free tier exists; real pricing
+negotiated) but is built for demand forecasting — whether its licence
+permits consumer republishing is unverified and decides whether it is
+usable at all. SeatGeek's Platform API is real, free-keyed, US-leaning.
+
+**7. Attractions, as distinct from events**: the free, licence-clean base
+layer is [OpenStreetMap's Overpass API](https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Overpass_API)
+(`tourism=attraction|museum|viewpoint`, opening hours where mapped) joined
+with [Wikidata's SPARQL endpoint](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:SPARQL_query_service)
+(CC0 entities, coordinates, images, Wikipedia links) — the "free hour near
+me" gazetteer, and the machine version of the hand-curated list
+[festival-season/](../festival-season/README.md) said couldn't exist as a
+feed. For *bookable* attractions,
+[Viator's Partner API basic-access tier is free with no pre-authorization](https://docs.viator.com/partner-api/technical/)
+(search, availability, pricing, commission on referred bookings) — which
+also plugs into the affiliate lane
+[competitor-landscape/](../competitor-landscape/README.md)'s revenue
+analysis found empty among rivals; GetYourGuide gates its API behind 100k
+monthly visits and Tiqets behind partner contact; Google Places is paid
+per-request; Atlas Obscura is bot-blocked with no API.
+

+| Leicester (comedy festival, Feb) | Data Thistle; visitleicester.info; Skiddle | same UK API; detail-page scrape; API |

# product-wiki

Agent-maintained market, user, and competitor research for EdFringeNow, kept as
self-growing wikis under this directory (compile findings once, refine in place,
cite everything). This tree is **walled off from the app code** — nothing in the
repo may reference `product-wiki/` except the reviewed distillation under
`product-requirements/`, so no code silently depends on unreviewed research.

## What lives here

- **`product-requirements/`** — the human-reviewed distillation of the wikis into
  product requirements. The only `product-wiki/` content the rest of the repo may
  reference. Never auto-grown.
- **`sample-data/`** — small illustrative assets a wiki claim points to (created
  when first needed; never test fixtures).
- **Everything else** — wiki space. A wiki is a folder with a `README.md`
  carrying `## Sources`, `## Open questions`, and `## Growth log`. The weekly
  growth pass researches each wiki's own open questions and writes back cited.

## Wikis

- **[competitor-landscape/](competitor-landscape/README.md)** — the existing
  Fringe discovery/planning tools, split by which of the product's two questions
  they answer, and where each gap is.
- **[market-and-audience/](market-and-audience/README.md)** — festival scale, the
  overwhelm problem, and the two audiences the product targets: the live
  in-festival crowd and the trip planners.
- **[audience-divergence/](audience-divergence/README.md)** — where those two
  crowds' requirements pull apart, where they actively conflict, and the narrow
  spine they share.
- **[festival-season/](festival-season/README.md)** — the other Edinburgh
  festivals in August and across the summer: their scale, diversity, locations,
  the six different shapes an "event" takes across them, and whether the data is
  reachable.
- **[fringe-ticketing/](fringe-ticketing/README.md)** — who actually sells a
  Fringe ticket (the Society, the venues, edfest.com), the definitive operator
  census, why no third party can sell or earn commission on tickets, and why
  the edfringe scrape has no full replacement.
- **[festival-cities-beyond-edinburgh/](festival-cities-beyond-edinburgh/README.md)** —
  the same question pointed outward: which *other cities* carry the
  Edinburgh-in-August pattern, ranked by how close they are structurally rather
  than by fame, plus the candidate tail.
- **[comedy-festival-circuit/](comedy-festival-circuit/README.md)** — the
  worldwide comedy-festival circuit as a market: the annual census, which
  festivals are fringe-shaped (a real scheduling problem) vs showcase-shaped
  (a lineup, few stages), each one's organizer, ticketing and data
  reachability, and the trackers that follow the circuit.

1	# The Edinburgh festival season
2	
3	Everything else happening in Edinburgh alongside the Fringe — the other August
4	festivals, the rest of the summer, and the seasonal things that are not
5	festivals at all. Compiled once, refined in place.
6	
7	This page exists because the product's premise ("4,206 shows is too many") is
8	only true of one festival. In August the city runs at least eight programmes
9	concurrently, and they are not variations on the Fringe: they differ in scale by
10	two orders of magnitude, in how an event behaves in time, in whether a ticket
11	exists, and in whether the data is reachable at all.
12	
13	## Key insights
14	
15	- August is at least eight overlapping festivals, not one — the Fringe is ~80% of the events and all of the noise.
16	- One free API already carries all 11 festivals, with coordinates, start times, durations and prices.
17	- That API has no sold-out field — our sharpest live signal does not survive a move off the Fringe scraper.
18	- Its licence bars redistributing dumps to third parties, and we commit our data to a public repo.
19	- "An event" is six different shapes: daily run, short season, one-off, nightly anchor, drop-in, all-day occasion.
20	- The Art Festival is 40+ mostly-free drop-in exhibitions with no start time — a shape nothing in the product models.
21	- Summer starts in June: Hidden Door, the Meadows, the Carnival and Jazz & Blues all finish before the Fringe opens.
22	
23	## The August cluster (2026)
24	
25	Eight programmes overlap almost completely. Every one of them is running on
26	15–19 August; a visitor in the city that week is inside all of them at once
27	whether they know it or not.
28	
29	| Festival | Dates | Scale | Where |
30	|---|---|---|---|
31	| **Festival Fringe** | 7–31 Aug | 4,206 shows / 60,000+ performances / 299 venues / 74 countries | citywide |
32	| **International Festival (EIF)** | 7–30 Aug | 147 performances / 44 countries / 2 exhibitions | a few large halls |
33	| **Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo** | 7–29 Aug (not Sundays) | one show, ~800 performers, ~9,000 seats a night, ~230,000 a year | one venue |
34	| **Edinburgh Deaf Festival** | 7–16 Aug | 80+ events | Deaf Action + Fringe venues |
35	| **International Film Festival (EIFF)** | 13–19 Aug | 38 new features, 21 world premieres | 5–6 cinemas + pop-up |
36	| **Art Festival** | 14–30 Aug | 40+ exhibitions, 25+ partner galleries, mostly free | galleries citywide |
37	| **International Book Festival** | 15–30 Aug | ~600 events / ~600 writers / 41 countries | one campus, 3 rooms |
38	| **Fringe by the Sea** | 31 Jul–9 Aug | a small Fringe of its own | **North Berwick, not Edinburgh** |
39	
40	Two things fall out of the table:
41	
42	- **Volume is overwhelmingly Fringe.** Every non-Fringe August festival added
43	  together is roughly 900 events against the Fringe's 4,206 shows — the Fringe is
44	  ~82% of the cluster. (Corrected 2026-08-09: this read 3,649, the 4 June
45	  programme-launch figure, which was ~15% short of the delivered festival; the
46	  conclusion is unchanged and slightly stronger. See
47	  [market-and-audience/](../market-and-audience/README.md) for the correction.)
48	  Any ranking that sorts purely on relevance or proximity will show a Fringe-only
49	  city.
50	- **Scarcity runs the other way.** A Fringe show typically plays ~25 times. A
51	  Book Festival author appears once. An EIFF screening is often a single
52	  showing. The events that are hardest to replace are the ones the volume
53	  ranking buries.
54	
55	**Free Fringe (4–30 Aug) and Free Festival (6–30 Aug)** are not separate
56	festivals for data purposes — they are producers whose shows appear inside the
57	Fringe programme, so the existing catalogue already contains them.
58	
59	**Edinburgh Summer Sessions** (24–29 Aug per a listings aggregator, not yet
60	confirmed against a promoter source) is an outdoor concert series rather than a
61	festival programme, and is listed here only so a later pass knows it was
62	considered.
63	
64	## The rest of the summer
65	
66	The season starts in June and the pre-August festivals are almost entirely free
67	and outdoor — a materially different offer from the ticketed August cluster.
68	
69	| Event | Dates (2026) | Shape |
70	|---|---|---|
71	| **Hidden Door** | 3–7 Jun | pop-up arts festival, The Paper Factory |
72	| **Meadows Festival** | 6–7 Jun | free community weekend, one park |
73	| **International Children's Festival (Imaginate)** | May–Jun | children's theatre |
74	| **Jazz & Blues Festival** | 17–26 Jul | 100–170+ concerts (sources differ), clubs to concert halls |
75	| **Edinburgh Festival Carnival / Multicultural Festival** | 19 Jul | one-day city-centre parade |
76	| **Folk & Food Festival** | 24 Jul–2 Aug | free-entry food and folk, George Square Gardens |
77	
78	Outside the summer entirely, and named only so they are not re-researched:
79	Science Festival (April), Beltane Fire Festival (30 April), Storytelling
80	Festival (October), Hogmanay (December).
81	
82	## The seasonal city that is not a festival
83	
84	The brief's user — someone with a free hour — is not only choosing between
85	shows. Guide coverage of an Edinburgh summer converges on the same non-ticketed
86	list: Arthur's Seat and Holyrood Park, the Royal Botanic Garden, Inverleith
87	Park, the Meadows, Princes Street Gardens, Portobello beach (swimming), the
88	Water of Leith walkway, and the Saturday markets (Stockbridge, Grassmarket,
89	Castle Terrace).
90	
91	Two honest caveats:
92	
93	- **This is guide-site material, not a dataset.** There is no listings feed for
94	  "the Meadows is nice in August." Anything the product does here is a
95	  hand-curated short list, and should be sized accordingly. (Softened
96	  2026-09-01: for *attractions* specifically, OSM + Wikidata are a free
97	  machine-readable base layer, and the wider source landscape — for
98	  Edinburgh and every other festival city — now has its own page,
99	  [city-context-sources/](../city-context-sources/README.md). The claim
100	  stands for the curated "nice in August" judgment itself.)
101	- **The repo already has the seam.** `js/places.js` geocodes arbitrary
102	  non-show destinations through Nominatim, so a curated seasonal place is
103	  representable today without new infrastructure.
104	
105	## What "an event" means differs per festival
106	
107	This is the finding that matters most for design, and it is not a branding
108	question. Across the eight August programmes an event behaves in one of six
109	ways in time, and the differences change what the product can truthfully
110	promise:
111	
112	1. **Run** — repeats near-daily at one time across a long run (Fringe, Fringe by
113	   the Sea). Missing it today costs nothing.
114	2. **Short season** — a handful of dated performances, often at differing times
115	   (EIF theatre/opera/dance, larger Deaf Festival work). Each date is scarce.
116	3. **One-off** — happens exactly once (Book Festival author events, most EIFF
117	   screenings, Jazz concerts, talks). Missing it is terminal.
118	4. **Nightly anchor** — the same show every night, one venue, huge capacity,
119	   sold months ahead (the Tattoo). Behaves like a fixed commitment, not a
120	   candidate.
121	5. **Drop-in** — no start time at all: opening hours and a duration the visitor
122	   chooses (Art Festival exhibitions, typically ~10:00–17:00, mostly free).
123	6. **All-day occasion** — a single dated outdoor thing with no seat and no slot
124	   (the Carnival parade, Meadows Festival, Folk & Food).
125	
126	Only shape 1 is modelled today. Shapes 3 and 5 are the ones that break existing
127	assumptions hardest: a one-off is a point rather than a lane, and a drop-in has
128	no start time to reach in time for.
129	
130	## Locations
131	
132	- **The Fringe is citywide** (299 venues); everything else is concentrated.
133	- **The Book Festival is effectively one campus** — Edinburgh Futures Institute
134	  (1 Lauriston Place), plus McEwan Hall and, new for 2026, Greyfriars Kirk. All
135	  within a few minutes' walk of each other and of the Fringe's Bristo Square
136	  cluster.

Closes #567

Owner-directed research making the product-wiki ready for EdFringeNow's widened direction — a festival-planning product, not an Edinburgh-only one. Scope is `product-wiki/` only (nothing under `product-requirements/`). Built over three rounds of owner direction: the comedy-festival circuit from https://fromthecomicscomic.com/comedy-festivals/, then the planmyfestivals user guide + feature matrix + UI screenshots, then city-context sources + competitor revenue + a film-festival survey. Primary pages fetched first-hand throughout.

**comedy-festival-circuit (new page)** — the 85-festival 2026 census with computed run lengths and five tracker corrections; the parallel-volume × recurrence taxonomy (fringe-shaped vs showcase-shaped plus the structural exhibits); per-festival dossiers (organizer, recurrence, scale with launch-vs-delivered discipline, show model, venues, clash reality, ticketing platform, data reachability, concurrent festivals); the annual-vs-churn map; concurrent-cluster table; cross-festival ticketing/data ranking; tracker survey; **and a light film-festival adjacency** (Berlinale is film's fringe — public short-notice tickets, films screening up to 5×, an official favourites→iCal planner; tiffr is film's only third-party planner; Fantasia×JFL gives Montreal eleven shared film×comedy days). Headlines: **MICF is the southern Edinburgh** (803 shows / 9,164 performances, open registration, unauthenticated JSON APIs with per-performance sold-out flags); **Leicester's operating charity collapsed Aug 2026** with Feb 2027 contested; Leicester + Brighton share one open Eventotron API; **no machine-readable comedy-festival calendar exists anywhere**.

**city-context-sources (new page)** — where "what else is going on" gets published per festival city, sources not events: seven source classes with fetch-verified machine-readability; the per-country licensed-supplier market shape (**Data Thistle** covers Edinburgh+Brighton+Leicester in one free-registration API with per-performance prices; **ATDW** covers Melbourne+Adelaide at A$660/yr; **Eventfinda** covers Auckland+Wellington free); **Montreal's open-data portal publishes a daily-refreshed events calendar**; tourism boards have no APIs but their detail pages carry schema.org Event JSON-LD (one parser, every city); the closed-API graveyard (Eventbrite, Songkick, Fever/DICE, Time Out, Atlas Obscura); Ticketmaster Discovery + Skiddle as the free baseline; OSM + Wikidata + Viator's no-gate affiliate tier for attractions.

**competitor-landscape** — five passes: first-hand verification of all 2026 rivals; the empty field beyond Edinburgh; the **planmyfestivals user guide read in full** (a shipped cross-festival clash-free planner, invite-only, producer-funded — cross-festival moves to *claimed*, date-choice to *dented*, live reachability stays the one unclaimed axis); the **feature-comparison matrix** (11 tools × 9 axes) and **UI record** (12 screenshots under `sample-data/competitor-ui/` with provenance); and **How the rivals make money** — paid placement is the field's only earned revenue (edfringemap's posted £99–£749 rate card + sponsorship tiers including a local bars-food-venues tier; planmyfestivals' producer impressions with a VisitScotland footer credit), Plan My Fringe runs on donations, **no rival serves ads and none carries a travel-booking affiliate fingerprint** — our shipped partner links are alone in that lane. Corrections along the way: Ed Fringe Guide and Another Fringe Guide are byte-identical (one site); tiffr/Berlinale add film precision to the beyond-Edinburgh claim.

**fringe-ticketing** — the Listings-API approval question annotated twice: planmyfestivals (inferred consumer) and edfringemap (self-declared "official festivals API data") suggest the approval path is passable for planner/map-shaped commercial products.

**festival-cities-beyond-edinburgh** — JFL's "world's largest comedy festival" label corrected (~⅓ of MICF by ticketed shows); comedy detail deferred to the new page.

**market-and-audience / festival-season** — scope note for the widened direction; the "no listings feed" caveat softened with a pointer to city-context-sources.

All claims cited; launch-vs-delivered figures distinguished; NOT FOUND recorded honestly. `scripts/verify.sh` green (0 blocking) with all new pages tracked.

All three directions are researched, written, and on [PR #568](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/pull/568) — four new commits, verify green.

**City context ("what else is on") — sources, not events**, as asked. The market has a clean shape: it's a **per-country licensed-data business** — Data Thistle covers Edinburgh, Brighton *and* Leicester in one free-registration API with per-performance prices and booking links (it's the supplier behind VisitScotland and VisitBrighton — and already in our wiki as a competitor); ATDW covers Melbourne + Adelaide (A$660/yr, 30-day trial); Eventfinda covers both NZICF cities free. **Montreal is the outlier**: the city's own open-data portal publishes its events calendar as daily-refreshed CSV/GeoJSON. Tourism boards have no APIs anywhere, but their event detail pages carry schema.org `Event` JSON-LD — one parser covers every city. The open-API era is genuinely over (Eventbrite killed public search in 2020, Songkick takes no new keys, Fever bought DICE); Ticketmaster Discovery + Skiddle are the free baseline; attractions are solved free with OSM + Wikidata, and **Viator's affiliate tier is free with no gate** — which connects directly to the revenue finding below.

**Competitor revenue** — answered empirically (fingerprint-grep of every rival's fetched pages and bundles + their commercial pages): paid placement is the field's only earned revenue — **edfringemap publishes a full rate card** (£99–£299 stepped genre slots, £249 "moments", £749 spotlight, Stripe, "money never reorders the ordinary results") plus sponsorship tiers **including exactly the local lane you asked about** ("Bars, food & venues… in front of Fringe-goers nearby"); planmyfestivals sells producer impressions and carries a **"Supported by: VisitScotland"** credit; Plan My Fringe runs on donations. **Nobody serves display ads, and nobody — not one rival — has a hotel/flight/restaurant affiliate link.** The only product in the field monetizing travel affiliates is ours (the shipped footer's disclosed partner links). Bonus finding: Ed Fringe Guide and "Another Fringe Guide" are byte-identical — one site, two domains, corrected in the wiki.

**Film festivals** — surveyed light as instructed: **Berlinale is film's fringe** (274 films each screening up to 5×, public €9–15 tickets released 3 days out, an official favourites→iCal planner), then TIFF (with **tiffr**, film's only live third-party planner) and MIFF (18 days, in our MICF city, different months); IFFR/SIFF/BFI/Locarno/Sundance/Sydney/Busan complete the tier, and Cannes/Venice/SXSW-Film/Fantastic Fest fail the bar with reasons recorded. Repeat screenings split film's public majors from its premiere fests exactly as recurrence splits comedy — and Fantasia×JFL gives Montreal eleven shared film×comedy days.

```
product-wiki/city-context-sources/       NEW — source classes with fetch-verified machine-readability,
                                         per-country suppliers, per-city source table
product-wiki/comedy-festival-circuit/    film adjacency section (ranked planner-fits, failed-bar cases,
                                         cross-circuit facts)
product-wiki/competitor-landscape/       "How the rivals make money" (rate cards, sponsorships, the two
                                         empty lanes); guides-are-one-site correction; tiffr/Berlinale
                                         precision
product-wiki/fringe-ticketing/           edfringemap self-declares Listings API use — second consumer,
                                         stated not inferred
product-wiki/festival-season/            "no listings feed" caveat softened, pointer to the new page
```

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.

# product-wiki

Agent-maintained market, user, and competitor research for EdFringeNow, kept as
self-growing wikis under this directory (compile findings once, refine in place,
cite everything). This tree is **walled off from the app code** — nothing in the
repo may reference `product-wiki/` except the reviewed distillation under
`product-requirements/`, so no code silently depends on unreviewed research.

## What lives here

- **`product-requirements/`** — the human-reviewed distillation of the wikis into
  product requirements. The only `product-wiki/` content the rest of the repo may
  reference. Never auto-grown.
- **`sample-data/`** — small illustrative assets a wiki claim points to (created
  when first needed; never test fixtures).
- **Everything else** — wiki space. A wiki is a folder with a `README.md`
  carrying `## Sources`, `## Open questions`, and `## Growth log`. The weekly
  growth pass researches each wiki's own open questions and writes back cited.

## Wikis

- **[competitor-landscape/](competitor-landscape/README.md)** — the existing
  Fringe discovery/planning tools, split by which of the product's two questions
  they answer, and where each gap is.
- **[market-and-audience/](market-and-audience/README.md)** — festival scale, the
  overwhelm problem, and the two audiences the product targets: the live
  in-festival crowd and the trip planners.
- **[audience-divergence/](audience-divergence/README.md)** — where those two
  crowds' requirements pull apart, where they actively conflict, and the narrow
  spine they share.
- **[festival-season/](festival-season/README.md)** — the other Edinburgh
  festivals in August and across the summer: their scale, diversity, locations,
  the six different shapes an "event" takes across them, and whether the data is
  reachable.
- **[fringe-ticketing/](fringe-ticketing/README.md)** — who actually sells a
  Fringe ticket (the Society, the venues, edfest.com), the definitive operator
  census, why no third party can sell or earn commission on tickets, and why
  the edfringe scrape has no full replacement.
- **[festival-cities-beyond-edinburgh/](festival-cities-beyond-edinburgh/README.md)** —
  the same question pointed outward: which *other cities* carry the
  Edinburgh-in-August pattern, ranked by how close they are structurally rather
  than by fame, plus the candidate tail.
- **[comedy-festival-circuit/](comedy-festival-circuit/README.md)** — the
  worldwide comedy-festival circuit as a market: the annual census, which
  festivals are fringe-shaped (a real scheduling problem) vs showcase-shaped
  (a lineup, few stages), each one's organizer, ticketing and data
  reachability, the trackers that follow the circuit, and a light survey of
  the film festivals that share the shape.
- **[city-context-sources/](city-context-sources/README.md)** — where "what
  else is going on" gets published in each festival city: the source classes
  (licensed suppliers, open data, DMO calendars, discovery APIs, attractions
  layers), how machine-readable each is, and the per-city best reads.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- explore-link: Mine one given URL for product, market, usage and pricing insights and fold them into an existing product-wiki page — cited, dated, delivered as a PR. Use when the owner says "/explore-link <url>", or hands over a link and asks for it to be read into the wiki.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the tidy-repo pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production long enough to judge — is it working, misused, overused, underused — read from its real production record against expectations written down when the element was designed. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- static-site-releases: The release standard every static-site repo of ours ships — the date-anchored version scheme, release-on-push, the explicit publish set, .github/site.config, the vendored workflows, the Pages deploy, and the setup a new site repo needs. Use when setting up a site repo, changing or debugging its release pipeline or site.config, when asked to "bump version" on a site repo, or when a static-website check fires.
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".

As an aside - does the DocAviv festival also fit the mold? Or any other film festival in Israel?

I imagine the next evolution of EdFringeNow to be the planning tool for festival fanatics, who want to go to a festival, maximize their time there, possibly with time off, but still optimizing their stay, in a complex scheduling environment. We should certainly support non-festival activities (food, excursions, time off) when helping to plan, but the reason we'll be the tool to use would be handling the complexity. Festmaxxing.

Btw, if you can think of other non-festival environments that have the same charechteristics of time limitation, complexity and abundance - please offer them. Does fashion week apply? The olympics? Please extract the definition of the intended "festival-like" description and restructure the "candidate festivals" wiki using that definition.

input.description: Survey Israeli film festivals
input.prompt:
You are a research agent. Today is 2026-09-01. Your job: a LIGHT survey of Israel's film festivals, judged against a "planner-fit bar" (defined below). Report only — do NOT edit any files, do NOT commit anything.

CONTEXT: This is for a product-research wiki for a festival-planning product. The product's home turf is the Edinburgh Fringe (3,000+ shows, multi-venue, month-long, real scheduling conflicts). We already surveyed international film festivals: Berlinale (274 films, each screened up to 5×, public tickets €9–15, official favourites→iCal planner) and TIFF ranked as film's best planner fits. The owner now asks specifically: does Docaviv fit the mold? Any other film festival in Israel?

THE BAR (score each festival against these dimensions):
1. Time-boxed window — fixed dates, roughly a week or longer (not a weekend event).
2. Abundance — far more films/screenings than one person can attend.
3. Simultaneity — many screenings run at once, so real schedule conflicts.
4. Venue spread — multiple venues, travel between them a real constraint.
5. Repeat chances — is each film screened more than once in the window? (This is what turns triage into optimization.)
6. Open per-screening ticketing — can a member of the public buy a ticket to a specific screening (price?), vs industry badge / invite.
7. Anchored recurrence — annual, same city, largely same venues, since when.
8. City context — what else is on in the city during it (e.g. a festival during a national holiday week).

FESTIVALS TO COVER:
- Docaviv (Tel Aviv International Documentary Film Festival) — the one specifically asked about. Dates/length of the 2026 (or latest) edition, film count, screening venues (Tel Aviv Cinematheque + satellites?), repeat screenings per film, ticket prices, organizer, since when.
- Jerusalem Film Festival — same facts.
- Haifa International Film Festival — same facts; note it runs during Sukkot (holiday week — relevant to "time off" planning).
- Then briefly: any OTHER Israeli film festival of real size (TLVFest, Cinema South Festival Sderot, Utopia, Animix, Icon TLV, Epos, Solidarity — only the ones that turn out to be non-trivial in scale). One or two lines each is enough for the small ones.

EVIDENCE RULES (mandatory):
- Every factual claim carries the URL it came from.
- Tag each fact [F] if you actually fetched the page and read it, [S] if it comes only from a search-result snippet.
- Fetching: curl through the pre-configured agent proxy works for most domains in this sandbox (plain `curl -sS -L <url>` via Bash; save to /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-EdFringeNow/26ae9aec-41c3-56e6-b289-00b96b2f07a2/scratchpad/ if you need to read at length). WebFetch and WebSearch are also available (load via ToolSearch if needed). Hebrew-language sources are fine — read them directly.
- If a fact cannot be established, write NOT FOUND for it explicitly. Never estimate without labeling the estimate as yours.
- Festival sites often show the *upcoming* edition or a stale one — date-stamp what you read (which edition a number describes).

DEPTH CAP: this is a light survey. Per festival: up to ~15 fact lines + one verdict paragraph scoring it against the 8 dimensions and naming what fails. Do not build dossiers.

REPORT FORMAT: one block per festival — a fact list (each line: fact — URL [F|S]) then "Verdict:" paragraph. End with a 3-line overall answer: does Docaviv fit the mold, which Israeli festival fits best, and what fails across the board.

input.prompt:
You are a research agent. Today is 2026-09-01. Your job: assess NON-FESTIVAL environments against a "festmaxxing" definition (below), with verified facts. Report only — do NOT edit any files, do NOT commit anything.

CONTEXT: A festival-planning product (home turf: Edinburgh Fringe) wants to know which other environments share the Fringe's shape — time limitation, complexity, abundance — so a stay there is a genuine constrained-optimization problem. The owner specifically asks: does fashion week apply? The Olympics? And offer others.

THE DEFINITION (score each candidate on all 8):
1. Time-boxed window — fixed dates, roughly a week+ (a weekend plans itself).
2. Abundance — catalogue far exceeds one person's capacity.
3. Simultaneity — many options at once; every choice forecloses others.
4. Venue spread — scattered enough that travel time is a binding constraint.
5. Repeat chances — items recur within the window (optimization, not triage).
6. Open per-event access — the public can buy a ticket/slot to a specific item (not badge-only, invite-only, or one wristband for everything).
7. Anchored recurrence — annual (or fixed cycle) in the SAME city/venues, so data investment compounds.
8. City context — real non-event things around it (food, sights, rest).

CANDIDATES TO VERIFY (facts + citations for each):
1. Fashion weeks (Paris, Milan, NYC, London): Can the public buy tickets to runway shows at all? Establish the access model (invitations, industry accreditation), roughly how many shows/venues/days per week, and whether any public-facing ticketed programme exists (e.g. NYFW "The Shows" public tickets? CPHFW?). This is the owner's direct question — get the access answer solid.
2. Summer Olympics, Paris 2024 as the data point: number of ticketed sessions (~750?), tickets sold (~9.5M?), venue count and spread, days (~17), how tickets were sold (draw phases, packs, official resale), price range — and the structural fact that the host city rotates every 4 years (no anchored recurrence). One line on FIFA World Cup 2026 (multi-city, even more scattered) as contrast.
3. Gen Con (Indianapolis): total scheduled events per edition (~tens of thousands?), the badge + per-event-ticket model (generic tickets), days (4), venues, annual since 1968?, same city since 2003?
4. San Diego Comic-Con: badge-only model (no per-event tickets), concurrent programming scale (how many parallel rooms/panels), offsite activations open to public, whether third-party schedule tools exist.
5. Walt Disney World + TouringPlans.com: the commercial existence proof of paid itinerary optimization — what TouringPlans sells (subscription price?), what it optimizes (wait-time models, step-by-step touring plans), and the structural difference (a theme park is continuous, not time-boxed; the time box is the visitor's own trip).
6. Open House London (or Doors Open Days): scale (how many buildings), window (a weekend? longer?), booking model (free, ballots, timed slots).
7. Burning Man: the What Where When guide (how many participant-run events?), access model (one ticket, no commerce inside), window (~9 days), recurrence (same place annually).
8. NYC Restaurant Week (as the restaurant-week archetype): window (weeks), participating restaurant count (hundreds), the reservation-as-scarce-slot model.
9. CES Las Vegas: days, exhibitor count, badge model, venue spread.
10. OPTIONALLY offer 1–3 more environments you judge genuinely close to the definition (e.g. Salzburg Festival as a performing-arts season, Art Basel Miami week, SXSW is already known to us — skip it). Only with facts.

EVIDENCE RULES (mandatory):
- Every factual claim carries the URL it came from.
- Tag each fact [F] if you fetched and read the page, [S] if it comes only from a search snippet.
- Fetching: plain `curl -sS -L <url>` through the pre-configured proxy works for most domains in this sandbox (save long pages to /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-EdFringeNow/26ae9aec-41c3-56e6-b289-00b96b2f07a2/scratchpad/ and read from disk). WebFetch/WebSearch also available (load via ToolSearch if needed).
- NOT FOUND is a valid and required answer when a number can't be established. Never present an estimate as a source's figure.
- Date-stamp which edition/year each number describes.

DEPTH CAP: survey, not dossiers. Per candidate: up to ~12 fact lines + one verdict paragraph scoring against the 8 dimensions, naming exactly which dimensions fail.

REPORT FORMAT: one block per candidate — fact lines (fact — URL [F|S]) then "Verdict:". End with a ranked shortlist: which non-festival environments genuinely clear the bar, which fail instructively and on what.

- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- explore-link: Mine one given URL for product, market, usage and pricing insights and fold them into an existing product-wiki page — cited, dated, delivered as a PR. Use when the owner says "/explore-link <url>", or hands over a link and asks for it to be read into the wiki.

Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.

- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
